reports.games: Hearts of Iron IV (Paradox, 2016–present) and its designer DLCs: base-game Division Designer, Man the Guns (1.6, 2019) ship designer, No Step Back (1.11 'Barbarossa', 2021) tank designer + combat width rework, By Blood Alone (1.12, 2022) plane designer. Sources: hoi4.paradoxwikis.com (Division designer, Tank designer, Land battle pages), Paradox forum meta analyses incl. the community combat-width evaluation PDF (forumcontent.paradoxplaza.com/public/798717/CW_meta.pdf), Wargamer/PCGamesN coverage of the 1.11 width rework, Steam guides (Teng's NSB tank guide, 'Ultimate Guide to Division Templates, Aircraft and Tank Designs'), EIP.gg plane/ship design guides, and community meta threads on space marines, roach destroyers, and light-attack spam.

systems.domain: Division Designer (templates, battalions, support companies)
systems.how_it_works: Player edits a TEMPLATE, not individual units: a 5x5 grid of combat battalions (infantry, artillery, tanks, motorized, etc.) plus 5 support company slots (engineers, recon, signal, logistics, field hospital, flame tank, etc.). Every deployed division of that template shares it; editing the template retro-fits all existing divisions (triggering equipment demand and a temporary strength/org hit). Template edits cost Army XP (earned from combat/exercises/lend-lease), gating iteration. Each battalion contributes stats — soft attack, hard attack, defense, breakthrough, organization, HP, armor, piercing, combat width — and division org is the AVERAGE of battalions (why pure-infantry has high org and tank-heavy divisions need motorized filler), while most other stats are sums. Support companies add stats without adding combat width. Equipment needs are the sum of battalion needs (e.g. one infantry battalion = 100 rifles; artillery battalion = 36 guns).
systems.strengths: This is HoI4's single most beloved system and a huge driver of its 40k+ concurrent players: it creates player IDENTITY ('my 9/1s', 'my 7/2s'), makes doctrine tangible, and the template-level abstraction is genuinely brilliant — you design once and produce/deploy at scale, so 200 divisions never means 200 design chores. XP-gated editing makes design a strategic resource decision. Support companies create satisfying kit-bash decisions. The system makes army composition a creative act rather than a picklist.
systems.weaknesses: Solved-game syndrome: because combat math is deterministic and opaque, the community reduces the entire possibility space to 2-3 'correct' templates per era (7/2 infantry, 40-width tanks, later 9/1 and 15w/42w), and anyone not reading external guides is simply worse at the game with no in-game way to learn why. Stats like breakthrough vs defense are never explained in-game; the org-average rule is invisible; new players bounce hard. Retro-fit-everything editing means one global template change mid-war, which is powerful but ahistorical (no legacy equipment pools in the field). Meta discovery lives on YouTube/Reddit, not in the game.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the template abstraction wholeheartedly — it is the right shape for 'design your own units' at grand-strategy scale and fits our real-time-with-pause, 4,600-province game: design formations/regiments once, instantiate many. ADAPT three things: (1) make the combat math legible IN-GAME — show a predicted engagement outcome vs a reference opponent when designing (our hourly-tick sim can literally run a preview battle); (2) replace free retro-fitting with generational re-equipment programs that take time and industrial capacity — a 1955 Soviet motor-rifle division upgrading to BTRs should be a visible multi-year program, which fits our cohort/industry economy; (3) for a Cold War game, templates should be per-DOCTRINE-GENERATION (Pentomic army, motor-rifle reform) with big identity-defining choices, not a 25-slot grid of marginal swaps. AVOID XP-as-currency; use time + budget + political capital instead, since our wars are rarer and smaller than WWII.

systems.domain: Land combat math (org vs strength, soft/hard attack, breakthrough/defense, armor/piercing, terrain)
systems.how_it_works: Each division has Organization (will to fight) and Strength/HP (men+equipment). Combat resolves hourly: each side rolls attacks; attacker's soft/hard attack (soft attack vs unarmored targets, hard vs armored, weighted by target 'hardness') generates hits; defender's DEFENSE stat blocks attacks at only 10% hit chance, attacks exceeding defense hit at 40% — a 4x damage cliff. The attacker uses BREAKTHROUGH the same way when being shot back at. Hits damage org and strength; a division retreats at 0 org, dies if strength hits 0 or it can't retreat (encirclement). Armor > enemy piercing → attacker's attacks halved and the armored side gets bonus; this is the cliff that created space marines. Terrain multiplies attack/movement (mountains -60% attack etc.) and sets combat width: pre-1.11 all combats were 80 base width (+40 per flank), making 40w divisions optimal everywhere; 1.11 varied width by terrain (plains 90, forest 84, mountain 75...), softened over-width penalties, and made damage spread across targets by width. Community analysis (CW_meta.pdf) found 10/15/27/41-45 widths outperform 18/22/25 — i.e., the meta re-solved itself within weeks.
systems.strengths: The org/strength split is the crown jewel: battles are usually decided by broken cohesion, not annihilation, so fronts move without armies evaporating, and encirclement (killing strength, not just org) becomes THE decisive maneuver. Soft/hard attack vs hardness gives combined arms real texture. Terrain genuinely matters. The system produces recognizable WWII-shaped outcomes from simple hourly arithmetic — very compatible with our hourly-tick architecture.
systems.weaknesses: Combat width is a mystery meta-number: an invisible bin-packing constraint that dominates all design yet is explained nowhere in-game; Paradox spent a whole major patch (1.11) fighting the 40-width meta and merely moved the magic numbers. The 10%/40% hit cliff and binary-ish armor cliff create knife-edge stat thresholds that reward spreadsheet play ('one more point of piercing doubles your damage'). Org-wall infantry spam is dull but effective. Damage is per-division-pair with little modeling of ammunition, ranged fires, or air-land integration beyond flat modifiers.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the org-vs-strength duality — for LIMITED war under escalation ceilings it is even more important than in HoI4: political will and unit cohesion breaking before physical destruction is the entire story of Korea and Vietnam; we should extend it with a third, national-level 'will' layer that ties combat results to our influence-warfare pillar. AVOID combat width as a hidden bin-packing number — HoI4's own patch history proves it just relocates the meta. Replace it with visible frontage per province edge derived from our real province geometry, shown on the map, with diminishing returns instead of cliffs. AVOID all threshold cliffs (10/40 hit chance, armor all-or-nothing): use smooth curves so +1 stat is always worth roughly +1 outcome — this single choice kills half the spreadsheet meta. Terrain multipliers: adopt as-is, they're cheap and effective.

systems.domain: Community metas and the patch arms race (40-width, space marines, and what they reveal)
systems.how_it_works: 40-width meta: because base combat width was 80, two 40w divisions filled a battle perfectly and concentrated stats; 40w was optimal in ALL terrain for 5 years until 1.11. Space marines: putting one heavy tank battalion in a cheap infantry division raised division armor (armor formula heavily weights the max-armor battalion: ~40% highest + 60% average) above typical AI/enemy piercing, halving incoming damage for trivial cost. Paradox fought it across years: special forces caps, scaling piercing (partial-pierce now does partial damage instead of nothing), fuel costs on armor (armor now consumes oil, limiting reach), and armor-formula tweaks. Each nerf produced a successor meta (light-tank marines, cheap flame-tank support companies giving huge terrain bonuses for <4 IC per tank, 'roach' filler). Meta knowledge lives entirely outside the game; MP lobbies enforce house rules banning known exploits.
systems.strengths: Honestly, the arms race shows engagement: people care enough to write PDFs evaluating combat widths. A designer WITHOUT exploitable depth would be a picklist. The metas also show players love cost-efficiency play (the roach, the 4-IC flame tank) — 'cheapest thing that works' is a fun axis, not just 'strongest thing'.
systems.weaknesses: Every degenerate meta traces to the same three root causes: (1) hidden formulas with thresholds/cliffs (armor-pierce, hit-chance, width), (2) stats averaged or max-picked across battalions letting one cheap battalion poison the whole formula (space marines exploit the armor MAX-weighting; org-averaging exploited by filler battalions), (3) singleplayer AI that never counters (AI never builds piercing, so armor cheese is free). Paradox's fix cadence (yearly) means each meta reigns for months and gets baked into community identity, then patch notes read as nerf lists — players experience design-by-whack-a-mole.
systems.lesson_for_1950: Three concrete rules for our designer: (1) NO max- or average-weighted formulas across sub-components — every stat a component contributes should be additive or smoothly diminishing, so a token battalion can't transform a division's class; (2) make the OPPONENT adaptive: our espionage pillar is the built-in fix — enemy intelligence should observe your designs in combat and procure counters over a doctrine-lag delay (armor cheese in Korea → enemy fields AT weapons by year's end), which turns exploits into temporary edges and makes espionage/counterintel matter for unit design; (3) embrace cost-efficiency as a first-class axis: show cost-per-effect in the designer UI, because 'MiG-15: 80% of the performance at 30% of the cost' IS the Cold War procurement story and the roach-players are our target audience.

systems.domain: No Step Back tank designer (chassis + modules)
systems.how_it_works: Pick a chassis (light/medium/heavy/super-heavy/amphibious, by tech year), then fill discrete slots: main gun (small cannon → high-velocity → howitzer, each trading soft vs hard attack vs breakthrough), turret type, suspension (Christie = speed, interleaved roadwheels = +breakthrough/reliability cost, torsion bar), engine type (petrol/diesel/gas turbine), armor type (riveted/welded/cast/sloped), and ~4 special slots (radios +breakthrough, wet ammo storage +reliability, easy maintenance, extra armor, flamethrower). Engine-power and armor are SLIDERS (0-15ish) trading speed vs armor vs cost. Each choice moves production cost (IC), reliability (chance to lose tanks to attrition/accidents), fuel use, and combat stats. Designs are saved as equipment variants; factories produce a specific design with production-efficiency retooling penalties when switching. The same chassis can be specialized into tank-destroyer/SPG/SPAA variants. Community meta: mediums exist only to deliver breakthrough (armor mostly ignored in SP since AI lacks piercing); cheap <4-IC flame tanks as support companies became mandatory in every infantry division; reliability modules (easy maintenance) outperform combat modules in long wars.
systems.strengths: The most successful of the three vehicle designers: discrete NAMED modules ('sloped armor', 'diesel engine') read as history, not spreadsheet; players genuinely recreate the T-34 or build cursed 'funny tanks' (super-heavy flame platforms) — expressiveness that generates community content. Reliability as a stat is inspired: it makes boring-but-sturdy a real archetype and cost a multi-dimensional tradeoff. Variant/chassis reuse maps to real procurement (one hull, many roles). Integration with production lines (retooling penalties) makes design timing strategic.
systems.weaknesses: Two sliders (armor, engine) reintroduce continuous min-maxing — the meta is 'minimum viable speed 4.0 km/h, dump everything into cost reduction', i.e., the sliders get set by formula, not by taste. Because the AI can't evaluate designs, singleplayer optimal play is armor-less cost-minimized boxes, which feels wrong. Stat soup: a tank has ~10 combat-relevant stats whose combat weights are opaque, so the designer is only as good as the external guide you read. Flame-tank support companies were an unintended dominant answer for years.
systems.lesson_for_1950: This is the closest model for OUR designer — ADOPT chassis + discrete named modules, and it maps beautifully to 1950-91: airframe generations (MiG-15 → -21 → -29), tank generations (T-54 → T-64 → T-72), each a chassis with engine/gun/armor/electronics/missile module slots, and mid-generation upgrade packages as variants. ADOPT reliability, and extend it into a maintenance/readiness burden fed by our economy (spare parts from industry, fuel from oil balance, trained crews from demographic cohorts) — Cold War arsenals were readiness games, not production games. AVOID free-floating sliders entirely: every choice should be a discrete module with a name, a story, and a visible tradeoff. ADD what HoI4 can't do: EXPORT designs — selling your fighter design to a client state is an influence-warfare action; captured/defected equipment (a MiG-15 landing in the South) is an espionage event that leaks module knowledge. Unit design then serves all four pillars, not just war.

systems.domain: By Blood Alone plane designer
systems.how_it_works: Airframes (small/medium/large + carrier-capable, by year: 1933/36/40/44) with weapon slots (MGs, cannons, bomb bays, torpedoes, rockets) and modules (engines x4 levels, armor plate, self-sealing tanks, drop tanks, radio navigation, radar). Key derived stats: air attack, air defense, AGILITY (dogfight positioning) and SPEED, thrust vs WEIGHT (over-weight designs suffer), range, and mission-specific stats (ground attack for CAS, naval attack for NAV). One airframe can be built as fighter/CAS/naval bomber depending on modules; missions (air superiority, CAS, port strike, logistics strike) are assigned by air region. Meta findings: small-airframe cheap fighters with max engines dominate (agility+speed scale winrate superlinearly in the air-combat formula); rushing 1940 improved airframes beats producing 1936 frames (+30% agility, +38% range, +22% air defense for marginal cost); dedicated CAS with max bomb bays; naval bombers were repeatedly the most broken thing in the game (cheap torpedo planes deleting fleets).
systems.strengths: Airframe-role flexibility is elegant — one good frame, many loadouts, exactly like real multirole procurement. Cheap-fighter-swarm vs quality-fighter is a real strategic choice with industry implications. Range as an emergent stat creates genuine map strategy (drop tanks to escort deep strikes).
systems.weaknesses: The most spreadsheet-y of the three designers: the air combat formula (agility/speed weighting) is fully opaque, so the community solved it into ONE correct fighter within weeks and every other module is a trap for newbies. Air combat itself resolves in abstract region-wide furballs, so design differences are felt only as attrition-rate deltas on a graph — you never SEE your design be good, which starves the fantasy. Stat-check gameplay: whoever read the guide wins the air war, then CAS wins the land war; air is the highest-leverage and least-legible layer.
systems.lesson_for_1950: For a Cold War game, air design is not optional — MiG Alley IS our Korea vertical slice — but AVOID BBA's abstract-furball resolution: with our hourly ticks and limited-war scale we can afford visible engagement events ('4 F-86 flights engaged 6 MiG-15s over the Yalu, 2 kills, 1 loss') so a design's qualities are experienced, not inferred from graphs. ADOPT airframe generations + loadouts; in 1950-91 loadout choice (guns → early AAMs → BVR missiles, ECM pods) is the era-defining design axis and gives us natural tech drama (Vietnam's missile-reliability crisis is a scripted-history goldmine). CRITICAL for our pillars: air designs should have few, LEGIBLE stats (speed, agility, radar, payload, range — five, not twelve) with the matchup calculator shown in-game, because air-power credibility feeds nuclear brinkmanship (bomber/interceptor design is deterrence posture, not just war-fighting).

systems.domain: Man the Guns ship designer
systems.how_it_works: Hull types (destroyer/light cruiser/heavy cruiser/battlecruiser/battleship/carrier/sub, by tech year 1922/36/40/44) with fixed slot layouts: battery slots (light/medium/heavy guns, torpedoes), plus fixed-function slots (engine, armor scheme, fire control, radar, AA, catapult, mine rails, depth charges). Ships are EXPENSIVE and slow to build (a 1940 BB ~ 2 years), so design decisions are near-irreversible; existing ships can be refitted in dock at cost. Naval combat splits fleets into screen line vs capital line; LIGHT ATTACK stat fires at screens, HEAVY ATTACK at capitals, torpedoes at capitals once screens die. Meta: 'light-attack spam' — heavy cruisers stacked with light cruiser batteries delete enemy screening lines, then torpedoes kill naked capitals; and the 'roach' — a 780-IC minimum destroyer (vs 2,418 for a combat DD) whose only job is to exist as a screen so your capitals are legal, absorbing hits by being numerous and worthless. Both dominated MP for years; lobbies ban them by house rule.
systems.strengths: Refitting is the best idea here: modernizing a WWI battleship with radar and AA is exactly right and very Cold War (the entire Soviet fleet story is refits and generational leaps). High unit cost makes each design decision weighty and each loss narrative — naval is the one HoI4 domain where individual UNITS (named ships) carry drama. Slot layouts per hull give real identity between hull classes.
systems.weaknesses: The targeting rules (light attack only hits closest group = screens) created the purest exploit meta in the game — roach spam and light-attack spam are not clever, they're formula abuse, and they've never been fully fixed, only house-ruled away in MP. Naval combat is also the least legible system in HoI4 (positioning, detection, engagement-decision rolls all hidden), so most players ignore navy entirely — a designer attached to a system nobody understands is dead weight. Design-around-the-damage-formula rather than around history.
systems.lesson_for_1950: The meta lesson is about TARGETING RULES, not ships: any deterministic 'X only shoots nearest Y' rule WILL be weaponized with sacrificial cheap units — if we have screening mechanics (and Cold War naval/air needs them: escorts, SAM belts, interceptor screens), make target selection probabilistic and make cheap chaff cost something ongoing (crews from our demographic cohorts, readiness budget) so a roach fleet bleeds the treasury and manpower pipeline. ADOPT named capital units with refit lifecycles — carriers/SSBNs as individually-named strategic assets fits brinkmanship perfectly (an SSBN on patrol is a deterrence token on the map). For 1950-91, the ship designer's deepest hook is that naval design IS nuclear posture: SSBN quietness vs ASW sensor generations is a real designer axis that feeds directly into first-strike-survivability math for the brinkmanship pillar.

systems.domain: Production integration (military factories, equipment, template demand)
systems.how_it_works: Military factories are assigned to production LINES, each producing one equipment design; lines gain production efficiency over time (starting ~10%, growing toward 100%) and lose a chunk when switched to a new design (less if same family/chassis). Equipment flows into a national STOCKPILE; deployed divisions draw reinforcement/upgrades from it by priority; template edits or new deployments create demand spikes. Attrition and combat losses consume equipment continuously, so war is a duel of production curves. Resources (steel, tungsten, oil, rubber...) are per-line input requirements — missing resources slash output. Lend-lease ships equipment abroad. Licenses let you produce another nation's designs at a penalty. Convoys/fuel constrain projection.
systems.strengths: The production-line efficiency mechanic is quietly the best economic design in HoI4: it makes 'when do I switch to the new tank' an agonizing real decision (the 1936-vs-1940-airframe debate exists BECAUSE of retooling), rewards standardization, and punishes design churn — it is the natural predator of design-spam. Stockpile-mediated demand means the military economy and the designer are one system, not two screens. Equipment attrition makes limited wars economically legible (Korea consumes trucks and shells, visibly).
systems.weaknesses: Line micromanagement scales badly (late-game USA = dozens of lines to babysit); the stockpile is a black box that silently starves the wrong units; players learn to game efficiency retention rules; and because HoI4's whole economy IS the war economy, there is no peacetime tension — nothing else competes for those factories, so 1936-39 is just optimal build-order rehearsal.
systems.lesson_for_1950: We are better positioned than HoI4 here and should lean into it: our economy already has civilian demands (cohorts, power grids, steel/coal/oil balances), so ADOPT production lines with efficiency/retooling but make the REAL cost of a new unit design the guns-vs-butter fight — every MiG generation is steel and engineers taken from consumer goods, which is literally the systems-competition pillar (Soviet overspend as a loseable long game). ADOPT license/export production and extend it: arms transfers to proxies should be our influence-warfare currency (who equips Egypt in 1956 is a design-and-production decision). ADAPT the stockpile into visible theater-level pipelines for limited wars — Korea draws from a Far East depot with shipping lag, so a limited war stresses logistics without mobilizing the whole economy, keeping total war as the failure state. AVOID per-line micromanagement at 41-year scale: budget-level allocation ('30% of military industry to air') with lines auto-managed inside it, and hand-tuning only for the designs the player cares about.

key_takeaways: Template-level design (design once, instantiate many) is the proven correct abstraction for player-designed units at grand-strategy scale — adopt it; the failures of HoI4 are all in the combat-math layer underneath, not the designer concept.

Every degenerate HoI4 meta (40-width, space marines, roach destroyers, light-attack spam) traces to one of three root causes we can design out from day one: hidden threshold/cliff formulas (10%/40% hit chance, binary armor-pierce), non-additive stat aggregation (armor max-weighting, org averaging) that lets one cheap component poison a formula, and deterministic targeting rules that reward sacrificial chaff. Use smooth curves, additive-only aggregation, probabilistic targeting, and ongoing upkeep costs on cheap units.

Discrete NAMED modules (NSB tank designer) beat continuous sliders every time: sliders get solved into a formula, modules get solved into stories. For 1950-91 the natural frame is design GENERATIONS (MiG-15→21→29, T-54→64→72) with mid-life upgrade variants and refits (MtG's best idea), where retooling/production-efficiency costs are the built-in brake on design spam.

Make the counter-meta systemic instead of patch-driven: HoI4 exploits persist because the AI never adapts. Our espionage pillar is the fix — enemies observe your designs in combat and procure counters after a doctrine lag, turning every exploit into a temporary edge and making unit design a move in the intelligence war.

Unit design in a Cold War game must serve all four pillars, not just combat: exported designs are influence-warfare currency (who arms Egypt), bomber/SSBN/interceptor design IS deterrence posture for the brinkmanship pillar, stolen/defected designs are espionage events, and every new generation is a guns-vs-butter withdrawal from the civilian economy — which our existing cohort/steel/oil/grid simulation can price for real, giving us the peacetime tension HoI4 structurally lacks.

Legibility is the anti-spreadsheet weapon: HoI4's designers are beloved where choices read as history and hated where winning requires external guides. Keep combat-relevant stats per unit to ~5, show an in-game engagement preview against a reference opponent in the designer itself, and make limited-war engagements visible discrete events (MiG Alley kill reports) so players FEEL their designs work — org-vs-strength (cohesion breaks before annihilation) plus a national-will layer is the right combat core for wars fought under escalation ceilings.
