Sources consulted: rtw2.fandom.com/wiki/Design, navalgazing.net RTW2 series and Washington Treaty analysis, Matrix Games forums (treaty mechanics threads), aurora4x.fandom.com, Sufficient Velocity Aurora/RTW threads, civilization.fandom.com Design workshop (SMAC), strategywiki SMAC/Units, Steam community Stellaris auto-design discussions.

systems.domain: Rule the Waves 2/3 — warship design as the whole game
systems.how_it_works: You are Grand Admiral of one navy, 1890-1955 (RTW3: to 1970). Per ship class you set: hull type (BB/BC/CA/CL/DD/CV...), displacement, speed, main/secondary/tertiary battery caliber and turret layout, armor by location (belt, deck, turret, conning tower, torpedo bulkheads), range/endurance, freeboard, machinery type, fire control, and later radar/AA/missiles. Every choice consumes computed weight against displacement; the designer rejects infeasible hulls and applies legible penalties (e.g. 'cramped quarters' cuts accommodation tonnage ~30% and bleeds morale when deployed abroad). The knobs sit inside four outer constraints: (1) an annual budget set by politics and events, (2) dock-size caps on max displacement until you invest in infrastructure, (3) naval treaties that impose fleet tonnage totals plus per-ship displacement/caliber caps on NEW builds (Washington-style 35,000t/16in; treaties dissolve when war breaks out), (4) time — ships take 2-4 years to build and serve 20+, and you cannot see rival designs before you fight them. Combat runs in a tactical engine where your paper decisions get tested; after-action reports show which shells penetrated which armor at what range.
systems.strengths: Revered because every knob is a real, reasonable-about historical tradeoff, and because scarcity makes maximization impossible — design is allocation, not shopping. The killer loop: design is a multi-year BET against an unseen opponent; you fight 1935 battles with 1920 hulls (the legacy-fleet problem), so there is no solved build across a 60-year campaign. Failure is legible and instructive: 'my belt was pierced at 12,000 yards' directly authors the next class. Players name ships, mourn them, and write AARs — the design system generates narrative, not just stats.
systems.weaknesses: 1990s Windows-forms spreadsheet UI; opaque internal formulas force wiki dependence. Known metas exist per era (speed-plus-big-guns battlecruiser abuse early, all-or-nothing armor once unlocked, RTW2 destroyer torpedo spam) partly because the AI designs worse ships than players. Successor-class churn is tedious — you redesign near-identical ships every few years and manage refits across dozens of classes. Tactical battles can drag for hours of time-compression.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT — this is the closest spiritual template for our game, but port the CONSTRAINT ARCHITECTURE, not the knob count. Cold War maps one-to-one: multi-year design cycles (MiG-15→21, T-54→T-64), arms-limitation treaties as design caps (a SALT analogue constraining warhead counts/tonnage is native to our brinkmanship pillar), and defense budgets that should draw directly on our existing steel/industry/military-allocation sim — RTW fakes its economy, we already have a real one. Adopt wholesale: (a) lead time + service life so designs are commitments (a 1953 tank design fields in 1956 and fights in 1968), (b) opponent-design fog broken only by espionage, (c) RTW-grade legible after-action reports ('your T-54 glacis was defeated by 20pdr APDS at 1,200m') so limited wars like Korea function as live-fire intelligence on your design bureau. Avoid its per-class micromanagement: fewer, doctrine-level design decisions on our 4,600-province scale.

systems.domain: Aurora 4X — component-level design, where depth becomes impenetrable
systems.how_it_works: Freeware passion project; you design COMPONENTS before ships. Engines: choose a power multiplier (~0.1x-3x) trading speed vs fuel efficiency vs thermal signature. Active sensors: pick resolution (tuned to a target-size class) vs range. Fire controls: range and tracking-speed multipliers. Missiles: allocate size points among warhead, fuel, agility, engine per individual missile design. Each component is its own research project consuming a specific scientist's lab-time. Ships are then lists of finished components, with tonnage, crew, maintenance life, deployment time all derived. Effectively hundreds of interacting parameters, presented as raw database forms with no tutorialization; correct play requires out-of-game spreadsheets and the wiki.
systems.strengths: The deepest doctrine expression in the genre: missile navies, beam navies, fighter doctrines, and sensor/ECM warfare all EMERGE from component choices rather than being scripted. Component reuse creates authentic tech lineages (the same engine family powering three ship generations). Total realization of the 'you are the design bureau' fantasy; a devoted community has played it for 15+ years.
systems.weaknesses: The case study in when depth becomes impenetrable, and the failure has a precise anatomy: (1) two-layer design (design the engine, THEN the ship) doubles cognitive load and separates cause from effect; (2) knobs whose consequences cannot be evaluated without external math (sensor resolution vs target size is a formula, not an intuition); (3) feedback loops measured in real-world hours before a design is validated; (4) zero in-game guidance. Result: an audience of thousands, not millions, and fan projects (Pulsar4x) whose entire purpose is making it usable. Micromanagement of freight, colonies, and maintenance compounds it.
systems.lesson_for_1950: AVOID the two-layer component pre-design entirely — one design layer only; never 'design the engine, then the tank.' Aurora's diagnostic test is the useful export: a knob is legitimate only if a player can predict its consequence from the fiction alone (thicker armor = heavier = slower is self-evident; 'sensor resolution 32' is homework). Apply that test to every slider we ship. But STEAL its one triumph: the design space must be wide enough that US and USSR players can express opposed doctrines — quality-vs-mass, gun-vs-missile, quantity-of-cheap-airframes vs few exquisite ones — and have the war actually feel different. Depth of consequence, not depth of interface.

systems.domain: Alpha Centauri Design Workshop — the elegant classic
systems.how_it_works: A unit is exactly: chassis (infantry 1-move / speeder 2 / hovertank 3 / foil / cruiser / needlejet / copter / gravship — determines domain, speed, and what it may mount) + weapon OR equipment module (attack values 1-30, or colony pod / terraformer / probe team) + armor (defense values) + reactor (fission x1 to singularity x4 HP, also cuts cost) + up to two special abilities (AAA, drop pods, clean reactor, deep radar...; one until Neural Grafting). Roughly 4-5 decisions, ~34 components total across the whole game. The load-bearing mechanic is a SUPERLINEAR cost formula: high weapon + high armor + fast chassis together costs far more than the sum, so specialized units (unarmored attackers, unarmed garrisons) are cheap and do-everything units are ruinous. The game auto-generates competent default designs at each tech; the workshop is opt-in.
systems.strengths: The proven minimum viable knob count: four slots plus one cost rule yields role specialization, faction flavor, and real economic tradeoffs. The superlinear cost formula is a single elegant lever that kills the god-unit without a page of restrictions. Opt-in depth is the right accessibility model — casual players never open the workshop and lose little; enthusiasts live in it. Custom names and icons make designs feel authored and owned.
systems.weaknesses: Within each slot, components form a strict ladder (Gatling 5 obsoletes Laser 4), so the component PICK is never a choice — only the role allocation is. Weapons outscale armor over the tech tree, producing a late-game offense-dominant meta where defense is pointless. The workshop clutters with obsolete designs (manual pruning). Special abilities are unevenly balanced — a few near-mandatory, many never touched.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT as the skeleton of our unit designer, with its one flaw corrected. Structure: platform/hull class + primary armament + protection scheme + mobility/powerplant + 1-2 role specials — 4-6 decisions, superlinear cost coupling, competent auto-generated doctrine defaults so the workshop is optional mastery. The correction: make same-slot options LATERAL, not tiered — and 1950 hardware does this for free, because real Cold War kit was tradeoffs all the way down: 90mm high-velocity vs 122mm (penetration and ROF vs HE throw-weight), gun vs early ATGM, day/night optics vs cost, snorkel diesel vs nuclear boat, gun fighter vs missile-only interceptor (let players make the real F-4 no-gun mistake and learn from it over Vietnam). Concrete slots for a 1950 tank: weight class (light/medium/heavy — road/rail/bridge logistics implications on our province map), gun, armor scheme (cast vs welded vs later composite), engine, specials (stabilizer, IR sights, NBC sealing, deep-wading).

systems.domain: Stellaris ship designer — why players auto-best it (cautionary tale)
systems.how_it_works: Hull sizes (corvette/destroyer/cruiser/battleship/titan) carry section layouts with slot grids (S/M/L/G/H/X weapons; utility slots for shields/armor/hull; mandatory reactor/thrusters/sensors; aux slots). Components come in strict researchable tiers (Laser I→V, etc.) plus a rock-paper-scissors layer: kinetics strip shields, lasers melt armor, missiles/disruptors bypass defenses. An auto-design toggle regenerates designs on each tech advance. Combat is auto-resolved mass fleet battles driven by accuracy/evasion/penetration stats; the 3.6 'combat rework' (2022) attempted to sharpen the RPS counters.
systems.strengths: Genuinely accessible: the clearest slot-metaphor UI in the genre, cheap refitting, and the auto-design fallback is the RIGHT accessibility idea (SMAC had it first, done better). The RPS counter framework is the right instinct for making design situational rather than solvable.
systems.weaknesses: The community solved it, twice over, and the failure decomposes cleanly: (1) strict tiers mean half the 'choices' are non-choices — always mount the highest number; (2) the RPS layer only creates decisions if you KNOW the enemy loadout, but intel is shallow and mid-war refit is impractical, so counters collapse into per-patch dominant builds copied from the wiki (corvette-evasion spam, neutron-launcher artillery battleships, post-3.6 disruptor metas); (3) thousand-ship stat-blender battles make any single design's contribution illegible — no feedback authors the next design; (4) fleet COMPOSITION matters more than per-ship fitting, but the UI spends the player's attention on the wrong layer. Meanwhile the auto-designer is notoriously bad (persists with obsolete weapons — Steam forums are a decade of complaints), so the fallback punishes the players who most need it. Players either wiki-copy or auto-design; almost nobody 'plays' the designer.
systems.lesson_for_1950: AVOID its three sins, and notice the third is our biggest opportunity. (1) No strict tier ladders anywhere — every same-slot alternative must be a lateral tradeoff. (2) Never counters without intel: Stellaris has rock-paper-scissors but no scissors-detection, which is exactly backwards for us — ESPIONAGE IS A CORE PILLAR. Stolen blueprints, defector debriefs (the MiG-25 'Foxbat panic' vs the Belenko reveal), and Penkovsky-grade penetrations should reveal enemy design cards, making counter-design a live loop between the spy game and the workshop; deliberately feeding FALSE specs becomes counterintelligence gameplay for free. (3) Combat must attribute outcomes to design choices at readable scale — our limited-war structure (Korea vertical slice) is perfect: small, bounded engagements where 'MiG-15 outclimbs the F-80, rush the Sabre program' is exactly the historical experience. Fix its fallback sin too: our auto-designs must be genuinely competent doctrine templates, not garbage.

key_takeaways: Meaningful design = allocation under hard external constraints (weight/budget/treaty caps), never component shopping. Any strictly-better tier ladder is a future auto-solve (Stellaris); any unconstrained budget is a stat-max. RTW's designer is revered because scarcity forces identity: you can have speed, protection, or firepower — pick two. Our treaty pillar (SALT analogues) and real economy (steel, industrial allocation) should BE the constraint layer rather than faking one.

The minimum viable knob count is 4-6 decisions per design (SMAC's proof: chassis + weapon + armor + reactor + specials, with one superlinear cost formula replacing pages of balance rules). Depth should come from consequences and constraints, not slider count. Aurora marks the hard ceiling: the moment a knob can't be evaluated from the fiction alone, or design requires pre-designing components, depth becomes homework — one design layer only, every knob legible.

Design must be a bet against a partially-unseen opponent with real commitment: multi-year lead times, decades of service life, and factory retooling costs are what keep RTW unsolved across 60-year campaigns. This is natively Cold War — the MiG-15→17→19→21 generational cadence IS the mechanic, and a 1950-1991 span gives roughly 4-5 full design generations per domain.

Espionage is the missing ingredient that fixes the genre's counter-design problem: rock-paper-scissors only produces decisions when you can see the enemy's hand (Stellaris fails precisely here). Stolen blueprints, defector reveals, and combat-derived intelligence should feed the design screen — and planting false specs becomes counterintelligence gameplay for free. No other design-focused game has this loop; we get it from an existing pillar.

Close the loop with legible after-action feedback at the RTW grain: 'your T-54s were penetrated frontally by 105mm APDS at 1,500m' turns limited wars into live-fire R&D — which makes limited war under escalation ceilings (Korea) intrinsically rewarding rather than a consolation prize for avoiding total war. Stellaris's illegible stat-blender battles show what happens without this: design contribution becomes invisible and players stop designing.

Ship genuinely competent doctrine-flavored auto-designs (SMAC's opt-in model, executed better than Stellaris's broken one) so the workshop is optional mastery, and design the component space so US and USSR players can express opposed doctrines — mass vs quality, gun vs missile, cheap-and-many vs exquisite-and-few — as lateral tradeoffs that make their wars feel different, not as tech ladders.

reports.games: Wargame series (European Escalation / AirLand Battle / Red Dragon), WARNO, Steel Division 2, Armored Brigade (Matrix/Veitikka), Regiments (Bird's Eye), Flashpoint Campaigns: Red Storm, Hearts of Iron IV (No Steps Back tank designer), Rule the Waves 2/3, Shadow Empire

systems.domain: Wargame / WARNO deck building (national decks, unit cards, availability/veterancy)
systems.how_it_works: Deck building is a strategic pre-battle layer. In WARNO you pick a historical 1989 division (real ORBAT), get ~50 activation points, and buy 'cards' into categories (LOG/INF/TANK/AA/ART/AIR/HEL/REC); each additional card in a category costs escalating activation points, so breadth is taxed. Each card is a real Cold War platform (M1IP, T-72M1, BMP-2...) with a per-card availability count and a veterancy dial: the core tradeoff is quantity-vs-quality PER CARD — e.g. in Red Dragon roughly 8 Trained T-72Bs per card vs 6 Hardened top-tier tanks; up-vetting cuts availability ~25-50% per step. Veterancy buys accuracy modestly but suppression resistance/recovery massively. Red Dragon adds faction structure: national decks (one nation) get the largest availability/veterancy bonuses vs coalition/mixed decks that get wider toolkits; era-restricted decks trade modernity for mass (Category B = pre-1986 units, +5 activation points; Category C = pre-1981, +10 points). Specialization (Armored, Mechanized, Airborne, Marine) reshapes slot counts and availability multipliers. Crucially, no stats are invented by the player — every card is authored; 'design' means portfolio composition under scarcity.
systems.strengths: This IS unit design at the right altitude: players feel authorship ('my deck') without a stat-crafting minigame that can be solved. Real equipment names carry enormous fantasy weight — community metas are argued in terms of T-72BV vs Leopard 2A4, which is exactly the Cold War flavor we want. The availability/veterancy dial elegantly encodes NATO-quality-vs-WP-quantity as a PLAYER CHOICE, not a hardcoded faction stat. Escalating card costs create genuine opportunity cost. Era categories prove players will happily accept OLDER equipment in exchange for MORE of it — a mechanic, not a punishment.
systems.weaknesses: Red Dragon's mixed/coalition decks were widely called 'cancer' — combining best-of-both-blocs erased faction identity and dominated ranked; national deck bonuses never fully compensated. Balance lives and dies on hand-tuned point costs across 1000+ units — a forever-war of patches. Spam metas recur (cheap recon-infantry floods, helicopter rushes) whenever availability curves are mispriced. Deck building has a brutal new-player cliff: bad decks lose before the match starts. And the system is static — nothing in a match changes your deck; there is no campaign feedback loop, which is the layer a grand strategy game can add.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT as the core of our unit-design promise, relocated into the campaign. A player-designed 'expeditionary force' for a limited war IS a deck: the escalation ceiling is the activation-point budget (politics sets how many points you may commit to Korea; going over IS escalation), categories map to arms, cards draw on the national equipment inventory the industry layer already produces, and availability per card is literally how many airframes/hulls the stockpile and production lines can sustain in-theater. Veterancy comes from our demographic cohorts (reservists vs career soldiers vs veterans of the last war) instead of a free dial. Forbid nothing-personal mixed decks by construction: you field YOUR bloc's inventory plus whatever you've exported/lend-leased to clients — which turns the mixed-deck 'cancer' into an influence-warfare feature (arming a client IS building their deck).

systems.domain: Steel Division 2 phase system (time-phased availability)
systems.how_it_works: Every deck slot is assigned to Phase A, B, or C (A and B last 10 minutes each, C until match end); divisions have authored phase profiles ('early-rush' divisions front-load power in A, 'late' divisions are weak early and monstrous in C). Income schedules are a second dial: Balanced 110/130/155 points/min across A/B/C, Vanguard 140/125/90, Maverick 120/170/80, Juggernaut 110/115/175. Force composition is therefore a bet on WHEN the battle will be decided.
systems.strengths: Turns time itself into a deck-building resource; creates rock-paper-scissors between tempo profiles rather than raw stat comparisons; models real operational logic (recon screens first, heavy echelons later) almost for free.
systems.weaknesses: Beta reception was hostile ('terrible new ABC phase system') because phase-locking felt arbitrary in a 40-minute skirmish; Phase-A rush metas dominated whenever early income was mispriced; adds a full extra dimension to an already steep deck-building learning curve.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT the concept, discard the fixed timer. At campaign scale with hourly ticks, 'phases' become mobilization echelons: standing forces (Phase A), mobilized reserves arriving over weeks (B), war-economy output arriving over months (C). This is the honest way to express WP doctrine (colossal echeloned reserves, Category I/II/III readiness divisions) vs NATO (high-readiness standing forces, thin depth) — as reinforcement-flow curves fed by our existing demographic cohorts and industry allocation, not as stat modifiers. Korea slice: the phase profile of an intervention (what can arrive in month 1 vs month 6) should be the player's central operational question, exactly as Phase C divisions in SD2 must survive until their power arrives.

systems.domain: Armored Brigade / Regiments (roster construction and the date slider as generation model)
systems.how_it_works: Armored Brigade: pick faction (7 nations, 947 ground units + 149 aircraft), pick a DATE on a 1965-1991 slider, pick force type (infantry/mechanized/armored — which sets point budget shape), then buy units from a flat point-priced list. The date gates unit availability AND sets training/morale levels per nation-year — the same Soviet faction bought in 1968 vs 1985 is a different army (T-62s with poor thermal-less night fighting vs T-80s), with no tech tree at all: the calendar is the tech tree. Regiments deliberately removes free-form deck building: you pick an authored regiment composed of up to 3 Task Forces, and mid-battle the game periodically (~every 5 min) offers a choice of ~10 attachment packages to reinforce with — curated composition, drip-fed choice.
systems.strengths: Armored Brigade's date slider is the cheapest possible equipment-generation model that works: one scalar unlocks/retires everything coherently, and nation-year training values encode doctrine quality without any per-unit fiddling. Regiments proves that CURATED choice (pick among authored packages) retains most of the agency of deck building at a fraction of the balance surface and onboarding cost — its reviews praise coherent, historical-feeling forces.
systems.weaknesses: Armored Brigade's flat 947-unit purchase list is menu tedium incarnate — informative, but reviewers note buying is a spreadsheet crawl, and nothing you buy persists (single-battle scale, no campaign consequence). Regiments' curation means zero player authorship of equipment — it fails our hard requirement if taken alone; its Steam forums' most-asked question is literally 'does this game have deck building?' (answer: no, and a vocal cohort bounced off for that reason).
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the calendar-as-tech-tree backbone: our 1950-1991 span should gate historical equipment by date/nation as baseline (T-34/85 in 1950 Korea, MiG-15 vs F-86), with research spending merely accelerating/delaying entry by a few years — never inventing ahistorical branches. ADAPT Regiments' curated-package idea for the AI and for casual players: ship authored national TO&E templates (Soviet Motor Rifle Division 1965, US Pentomic Division 1957, ROAD 1963) that players can use as-is or open up and edit — template-first, blank-sheet-optional. AVOID the flat 900-item shopping list; the inventory must always be presented filtered through role and formation slots.

systems.domain: HOI4 tank designer (module-based stat crafting — the cautionary case)
systems.how_it_works: No Steps Back (2021) added a designer: pick a chassis (light/medium/heavy per generation), fill up to ~9 module slots (gun, turret, armor thickness slider, engine, radio, wet ammo storage...), each module trading soft attack/hard attack/armor/reliability/cost. Designs are then produced on production lines with efficiency ramp-up; divisions using template designs auto-upgrade as new equipment flows in.
systems.strengths: Enormous surface-level appeal — 'design your own tank' sells DLC and screenshots; integrates with production (a new design resets line efficiency, a real retooling cost, which is a genuinely good mechanic); variant/facelift system lets small changes keep partial efficiency.
systems.weaknesses: The canonical degenerate meta: because armor stats are checked against piercing in a binary-ish way and reliability is nearly free to ignore, the solved answer is a cheap chassis, maximum gun, ZERO armor, 0-20% reliability — one design for the whole war, every nation, every game. Paradox forums: 'unfun, immersion-breaking, kills the idea behind tank design'; players who experiment 'get punished and return to the meta.' Root causes worth internalizing: (1) too many knobs feeding too few effective stats collapses into one dominant point on the Pareto frontier; (2) no opponent-driven obsolescence pressure — the enemy AI doesn't adapt its guns to your armor, so armor never pays; (3) design decoupled from doctrine — nothing about HOW you fight changes what design is good.
systems.lesson_for_1950: AVOID free-form stat sliders; the failure is structural, not a tuning miss. If our players design units, every knob must map to a rock-paper-scissors axis the OPPONENT can shift: gun caliber vs armor generation, IR night equipment vs none, missile vs gun armament for interceptors. Obsolescence pressure must come from the other superpower's fielded designs (espionage reveals them — a direct hook into our intel pillar: stealing the T-64's armor spec should be a campaign event that invalidates your ATGM inventory). And KEEP HOI4's one good idea: new designs reset production-line efficiency, so churning designs has an industrial price paid in the steel/industry system we already simulate.

systems.domain: Rule the Waves 2/3 (unit design at strategic altitude done right — design cycle + obsolescence)
systems.how_it_works: RtW3 runs 1890-1970 at monthly ticks. Player designs every ship class: displacement, guns, armor scheme, machinery, later radar/missiles — but every parameter is bounded by CURRENT TECHNOLOGY, which advances semi-randomly under funded research, so the design space itself moves under you. Ships take years to build, serve for decades, and rot: engine wear runs on 10/20/30-year curves depending on engine type chosen at design time; old ships take an 'obsolete' debuff (worse flooding etc.) unless rebuilt — and a rebuild (new fire control, AA, machinery refit to hold speed) competes for the same budget and dock capacity as new construction. Fleet management is explicitly about staggering construction cohorts so the whole fleet doesn't obsolesce at once.
systems.strengths: Widely considered the best unit-design loop in strategy gaming precisely because designs are BETS UNDER UNCERTAINTY about a 15-year future, not solvable optimizations: the 1920 battlecruiser you design meets the 1936 air threat you couldn't foresee. Obsolescence is the engine of the whole game economy — you are never done. Refit-vs-replace is a constant, meaty decision. Design mistakes create war stories, not reloads.
systems.weaknesses: Spreadsheet-dense UI; monthly-tick pacing means long stretches of nothing; the RtW model works because naval platforms are few, expensive and individually named — it does not naively scale to armies of ten thousand tanks; late-era (missile age) design is thinner and less loved than the gun era.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the philosophy wholesale, applied to CLASSES not individuals: a 'design' in our game is an equipment class (a tank model, a fighter model, a ship class) created from bounded, generation-gated components; it takes years from design to fielding (the MiG-25 answer to the B-70 that never came IS this mechanic); it equips formations for 15-30 years and can be REFIT (T-55 upgrades, F-4 avionics packages sold to allies) at industrial cost instead of replaced. The 41-year span 1950-1991 is exactly two-to-three full design cycles per category — the same cadence RtW proves is fun. Our hourly ticks are for wars; design/procurement decisions should surface at monthly cadence with alerts, RtW-style.

systems.domain: Shadow Empire model management (living with an inventory of old designs)
systems.how_it_works: Player designs 'models' (tank/gun/vehicle types) that accumulate over a long game. Each model carries a quality flag set by the player — preferred / accepted / TOLERATED / OBSOLETE — that drives all automation: replenishment only draws accepted+ models; 'tolerated' means units keep existing old equipment until destroyed but never receive more (natural attrition-driven phase-out); flagging OBSOLETE force-recalls the model from the field to the strategic HQ. Infantry can cheap-'upgrade' in place; vehicles must be 'replaced' with newly built stock. Mass-upgrade commands exist per-HQ.
systems.strengths: Solves the exact problem a 4,600-province game will hit: dozens of designs across 40 years without hand-touching every formation. The tolerated/obsolete distinction is quietly brilliant — it models real armies (reserve divisions on T-34/85s into the 1960s, National Guard flying F-86s while the active force gets F-4s) as an automation POLICY rather than micromanagement. Community threads on 'old model clutter' show even this system strains, which tells us where the ceiling is.
systems.weaknesses: UI-heavy and obscure (top forum questions are 'how do I get rid of models?'); force-recall on obsolete flag creates gotcha moments (front-line units suddenly stripped); model clutter still accumulates because nothing pushes players to consolidate.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT a cascade policy as the default and make it thematic: new designs go to Category-A / front-line formations, displaced equipment cascades automatically to reserves, then to clients and proxies via arms exports, then to war stocks — each step a policy slider, not a click-per-unit. This makes the export cascade an INFLUENCE-WARFARE mechanic (your obsolete T-54s are exactly what you ship to Korea-adjacent clients) and ties disposal to the espionage layer (exported kit gets captured and examined — the real MiG-15 story). Cap live designs per category (say 3-4 concurrent generations) to prevent Shadow Empire's clutter; retiring a generation frees a design slot, forcing the consolidation the player otherwise avoids.

systems.domain: Doctrine asymmetry — NATO quality vs WP quantity (Flashpoint Campaigns + Wargame economics)
systems.how_it_works: Flashpoint Campaigns models the asymmetry not in unit stats but in COMMAND TEMPO: asynchronous turns driven by each side's C3 state — a crack NATO brigade issues new orders roughly every 10 minutes, a Soviet reservist formation waits 20+; degraded HQs, distance, and fatigue stretch the cycle. The result: NATO plays an OODA-loop game of maneuver and dislocation against a slower but far heavier opponent, with neither side's units needing inflated stats. Wargame expresses the same asymmetry economically: WP cards carry higher availability at lower veterancy, NATO the reverse, and the player positions themselves on that curve. Cold-war analyses (CBO, NATO histories) confirm the real structure: Pact standardization + echeloned mass + Category I/II/III readiness tiers vs NATO's heterogeneous, higher-quality, logistics-heavy forces.
systems.strengths: Both mechanisms create asymmetry players FEEL in play (tempo, sustainability) rather than read in a tooltip; both avoid the lazy failure of '+10% Soviet HP'. Flashpoint's is the most praised doctrine model in the genre; Wargame's makes doctrine a deck-building economy.
systems.weaknesses: Flashpoint's variable turns are confusing to newcomers and only work at battalion scale with minutes-long turns; pure command-delay asymmetry can feel like 'playing the worse faction' if not compensated with real mass; Wargame's economic asymmetry is undermined the moment cross-bloc mixing is allowed.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT both layers. At the campaign tick: doctrine = order latency and plan rigidity (Soviet formations execute pre-planned operations powerfully but respond to new orders with delay; NATO formations re-task fast but burn more supply per combat power) — cheap to model with hourly ticks, no per-unit stats needed. At the force-design layer: doctrine defines the deck economics — WP designs are cheaper to mass-produce (fits our industry allocation: same steel, more hulls), NATO designs cost more but hold veterancy and readiness better. Doctrine should also gate FORCE STRUCTURE (division slot layouts: tank-heavy Soviet MRD vs balanced US ROAD), which gives the 'design your own division' feature national character for free. Never model doctrine as flat stat modifiers.

systems.domain: Equipment generations 1950-1991 without one-tree-per-weapon bloat
systems.how_it_works: The historical structure is strikingly compact: armor runs in ~4 generations (T-34/M4 wartime stock → T-54/M48 early-50s → T-62/M60 60s → T-64/72/Chieftain 70s → T-80/M1/Leopard 2 80s), fighters likewise (subsonic MiG-15/F-86 → supersonic MiG-21/F-104/F-4 → 4th-gen F-15/MiG-29), and each generation is defined by a handful of COMPONENT breakthroughs shared across platforms: gun/ammo (90mm→105mm L7→120/125mm smoothbore, APDS→APFSDS→HEAT evolution), armor (RHA→composite/Chobham→ERA), fire control (stadia→ranging MG→laser+ballistic computer→thermal), propulsion, and for aircraft: engines (centrifugal→axial→turbofan), radar/missiles (gun-only→rear-aspect IR→all-aspect+BVR SARH). Games that model this well (Armored Brigade, Wargame's authored rosters) never tree it per-weapon; games that tree per-weapon (classic HOI research spam) drown in clicks.
systems.strengths: Component-generation modeling gives ~6-8 tech tracks TOTAL (tank gun/armor/FCS, aero engine/radar/missile, electronics, nuclear delivery) instead of hundreds of nodes; every real Cold War platform is reproducible as chassis-role × component picks; espionage integrates naturally (steal a component generation, not 'the T-72').
systems.weaknesses: Risk: component picks can recreate the HOI4 solved-meta problem if components lack counter-relationships; purely component-driven stats can make nations feel samey without doctrine/industry differentiation layered on top; naming matters enormously — players must see 'T-62' not 'Gen3 MBT variant #2', so procedural designs need a historical-name matcher or player naming.
systems.lesson_for_1950: This is our recommended architecture — three layers. (1) COMPONENT TECH: ~6-8 generation ladders advanced by research funding + espionage, date-anchored to history ±5 years. (2) DESIGN BUREAU: player creates a small number of equipment designs (capped slots per category) as chassis-role + component choices — RtW-style bounded bets with multi-year development, prototype events, and production-line retooling costs paid in our existing steel/industry system. (3) FORCE COMPOSITION: Wargame-style deck building of divisions/wings from the resulting national inventory, with availability set by stockpiles+production, veterancy by demographic cohorts, slots by doctrine, and total commitment to any limited war capped by the escalation ceiling. Obsolescence cascades (front-line → reserve → export → proxy) close the loop into influence warfare. This satisfies the director's design-your-own-units requirement with roughly the balance surface of 8 tech tracks and a few dozen concurrent designs — instead of 4,600 provinces × 40 years × per-weapon trees.

key_takeaways: Deck building IS unit design at grand-strategy altitude: let players design equipment classes (few, bounded, RtW-style bets) and then compose forces from the resulting inventory (Wargame-style cards with availability/veterancy tradeoffs). Two altitudes, both authored by the player, neither a stat-slider minigame.

Map Wargame's activation points onto the escalation ceiling: the political layer grants a commitment budget for each limited war, and the expeditionary 'deck' the player builds against it makes brinkmanship and force design the same decision. This is the single cleanest fusion of our pillars and the vertical slice.

The calendar is the tech tree (Armored Brigade's proof): gate historical equipment generations by date via ~6-8 shared component ladders (gun, armor, FCS, engine, radar, missile...), with research money and espionage shifting entry by a few years. Never build one tree per weapon; never let players invent ahistorical stat combinations.

HOI4's tank designer is the anti-pattern: free-form module sliders with no opponent-driven counter-pressure collapse to one solved design. Every design knob must sit on an axis the enemy's fielded (and spied-upon) designs can invalidate — obsolescence pressure must come from the other superpower, and design churn must cost production-line efficiency in our existing industrial model.

Model doctrine as economics and tempo, never stat modifiers: WP = cheaper mass-production, echeloned mobilization phases, order latency with powerful pre-planned operations; NATO = expensive quality, high readiness, fast re-tasking, heavier logistics. Flashpoint Campaigns' command-cycle asymmetry and Steel Division 2's phase profiles are the two proven mechanizations, both cheap to express at hourly ticks.

Automate obsolescence as a cascade policy (Shadow Empire's lesson, thematized): new designs to front-line formations, displaced equipment auto-flows to reserves, then to arms exports and proxies, then to war stock. This kills micromanagement at 4,600-province scale AND turns retiring your T-54s into an influence-warfare and espionage mechanic — which is exactly how the real Cold War armed its proxy conflicts.

reports.games: Primary corpus: Hearts of Iron IV (Paradox, 2016–present; hoi4.paradoxwikis.com Land_battle, PDX forum combat-width meta threads), Europa Universalis IV (eu4.paradoxwikis.com Land_warfare), AGEOD engine titles (AACW, To End All Wars; AGEWiki "Combat Explained"), Unity of Command 1/2 (2x2 Games; Game Developer design case study, official dev diaries on the supply network), Decisive Campaigns: Barbarossa (VR Designs / Vic Anthonis + Cameron Harris), classic hex-and-counter CRTs (SPI/Avalon Hill lineage, Wikipedia Combat_results_table, BGDF design threads, "Death to the Combat Results Table"), Lanchester attrition laws (Ernest Adams' Gamasutra "Kicking Butt by the Numbers", AAAI StarCraft Lanchester-prediction paper), plus Gary Grigsby's War in the East 2 (logistics/encirclement reference) and Rule the Waves 3 (unit-design-vs-resolution cautionary case).

systems.domain: HoI4 hourly combat math (continuous attrition at grand-strategy scale)
systems.how_it_works: The only shipped model at our exact scale and tick rate. Combat is a persistent battle object per contested province, resolved every hour. Each division generates attacks = (1−Hardness)·SoftAttack + Hardness·HardAttack, batched in groups of 10. Defender's Defense (or Breakthrough when attacking) 'blocks' attacks: blocked attacks hit 10%, unblocked hit 40%. Each hit rolls small dice (d4 for organization damage, d2 for strength), scaled by constants (~0.053 org, ~0.05 str). Two damage tracks: Organization (fast-recovering will-to-fight; hitting 0 forces retreat and ends the battle) and Strength (men/equipment; slow to replace, feeds back into industry). Armor>Piercing halves damage taken and boosts damage dealt. Combat width caps how many divisions fit per battle (post-No-Step-Back ~75–96 base, +flanking bonus per extra attacking direction, stacking penalty beyond the cap). Every 12h each side semi-randomly draws a 'tactic' (Breakthrough, Elastic Defense, Encirclement...) weighted by general skill and doctrine, multiplying width/damage. Only active battles compute — thousands of idle provinces cost nothing.
systems.strengths: Proven performant at ~13k provinces with hourly ticks; battles-as-persistent-objects means RTwP works naturally (pause, inspect, redeploy). Org-vs-Strength split is the single best idea in the genre: battles end by cohesion collapse, not annihilation, so fronts move without armies evaporating, and encirclement is what actually kills equipment (pocketed units that retreat with 0 org into enemy territory are destroyed). Division templates feed straight into these stats, making unit design legible: the player can read soft attack/org/width and understand why a design wins. Emergent encirclements from province adjacency are genuinely satisfying.
systems.weaknesses: Notorious degenerate metas: combat-width optimization (20/40 pre-2021, 24-ish after) turns unit design into solving one integer program; 'space marines' (one heavy tank battalion poisoning a cheap infantry division's armor stat because armor is a weighted average abused at the margin); larger divisions singling out smaller ones in target selection. Mid-game devolves into WW1 grinding because defense+entrenchment+org regen outpaces attack until doctrine/armor tech spikes — many players find 1941–43 a slog. Front-line AI ping-pong (units shuffling laterally along battle-plan lines, a bug complained about since 2016) shows the danger of automating fronts badly. Combat is also opaque: the battle window shows modifiers stacked 15 deep and few players can predict outcomes without wiki math.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the skeleton: persistent per-province battle objects resolved hourly, two-track damage (call it Cohesion vs Strength), frontage caps per province edge, and only-active-battles computation — this is the correct architecture for RTwP/hourly/4600 provinces in Bevy (each battle is an entity; systems iterate active battles only). ADOPT tactics-draw as our main stochastic layer (it's flavorful, general-driven, and variance lives at the 12h scale, not per-hit — cheap and readable). FIX the known failure modes at the design stage: (1) make frontage a continuous terrain property, not a magic integer players can solve — and vary it enough (Korean mountain passes vs plains) that no single template dominates; (2) compute armor/piercing interactions per-battalion or as saturating curves, never exploitable weighted averages; (3) our limited-war frame actually helps the grinding problem — Korea SHOULD stalemate at the 38th parallel when neither side escalates; make grinding the visible cost that tempts players toward escalation (air interdiction, more divisions, nukes). That reframes HoI4's biggest weakness as our core loop.

systems.domain: EU4 dice + pips phases (discrete-battle stochastic model)
systems.how_it_works: Armies are stacks; when two stacks meet, one battle runs in alternating 3-day Fire and Shock phases. Each phase both sides roll a d10 (0–9); each unit deals casualties = (offensive pips + die + general skill + terrain/crossing modifiers − defender's defensive pips), divided by Military Tactics (0.5→~3.75 by tech) and multiplied by Discipline. Units carry fixed pip profiles (fire/shock/morale, offense/defense) baked into the unit type by tech group — no unit design. Morale damage runs in parallel and ends the battle: a side breaks when average morale hits 0, so battles usually end well before annihilation. Combat width limits front-row units; reserves reinforce.
systems.strengths: The d10 with ±modifiers is legible: players learn 'crossing a river at −1 vs a +2 terrain defender with worse general = don't'. Morale-as-ending-condition again avoids annihilation. High early variance creates drama and underdog chances; late-game tech compresses variance. Battles are discrete events, cheap to compute.
systems.weaknesses: Stack-vs-stack with no front means no operational geometry at all: no encirclement (except stackwipe rules), no exploitation, no supply-cutting — warfare degenerates to doomstack chess and carpet-sieging. The d10 swing (a 9-vs-0 roll can delete an equal army) feels like slot-machine warfare in a game where the player invested decades in that army. Fixed pips means zero unit design agency. Force-limit blobbing is the whole military meta.
systems.lesson_for_1950: AVOID as an overall model — discrete stack battles are fundamentally incompatible with front-line dynamics, and our whole conflict fantasy (limited war along a front, interdiction, encirclement at Chosin) requires fronts. But STEAL two things: (a) the legibility principle — every combat modifier should be expressible as a small named number the player can read pre-battle ('mountain −30%, winter −20%, air superiority +15%'), because our unit designer only creates agency if players can predict how a design performs; (b) morale/cohesion as the battle-ending resource, which we're already taking from HoI4 in stronger form. Also note EU4's cautionary tale on variance: with hourly ticks we get hundreds of resolution events per battle, so per-event variance self-averages — that's an argument FOR small per-tick dice (they add texture without swinging outcomes) and AGAINST any single large roll deciding a battle.

systems.domain: AGEOD engine (WEGO orders, cohesion-first resolution, command friction)
systems.how_it_works: Both players issue orders, then the turn (2 weeks–1 month) resolves simultaneously day by day. Battles resolve in rounds: each element (regiment-scale sub-unit) fires per its rate-of-fire against a frontage-limited engagement window; hits deplete both Hits (men) and Cohesion, with Cohesion falling much faster. Units at low cohesion take assault penalties (≤60% cohesion: −1% per 2 points below) and retreat when it collapses — battles are decided by cohesion, casualties are a byproduct. Leaders have activation rolls (a bad general may simply not move this turn), postures (offensive/defensive/passive), and 'March to the Sound of Guns' lets nearby corps join battles probabilistically. Supply and weather attrition typically kill more men than combat.
systems.strengths: The most honest operational model in the corpus: cohesion-primary resolution + command friction + attrition-dominant losses matches how real campaigns work (armies are wrecked by marching, weather, and supply, not battles). MTSG produces emergent multi-corps battles. Posture system gives strategic intent without micromanagement.
systems.weaknesses: WEGO with month-long turns is the opposite of our RTwP hourly structure. Resolution is a black box — the battle log is famously inscrutable, and players can't learn from losses. Leader activation RNG ('my army refused to move, again') is historically defensible and experientially miserable. Reviews note the engine's tactical model never adapted past 19th-century linear battle-lines. Weak AI; performance degrades badly at large region counts.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT the philosophy, not the engine: (1) cohesion falls ~3–5x faster than strength in our resolution — this single ratio choice is what makes fronts fluid instead of grindy, because breakthroughs come from cohesion collapse while armies survive to fight again; (2) make out-of-combat attrition (Korean winter, monsoon, interdicted supply) a first-class casualty source rivaling combat — it's period-accurate (Chosin) and it makes our logistics/economy sim the weapon it should be; (3) command friction belongs in our game but as political friction, not dice: ROE restrictions, escalation authorization delays, coalition caveats ('UN forces may not cross the Yalu') are the Cold War analog of activation rolls — deterministic, player-visible constraints rather than RNG. AVOID WEGO itself and avoid black-box resolution.

systems.domain: Unity of Command (supply-line-cutting as THE mechanic)
systems.how_it_works: Turn-based hex operational puzzles. Combat itself is deliberately shallow (attack/defense values, small dice, hits either kill or suppress steps). The signature system: supply radiates from railheads along rail/road with terrain-cost falloff; any unit out of supply for 1–2 turns has its steps starve — 'even powerful tanks simply melt before your infantry' (Game Developer case study). Therefore the game is not about winning battles but about which battles to fight: you punch a hole precisely where it severs the enemy's rail line, then the pocket dies on its own. UoC2 adds HQ-based supply throw and force-multiplier specialist steps.
systems.strengths: The cleanest demonstration that supply topology, not combat math, is what produces encirclement gameplay. Because a cut supply line is worth more than any stat advantage, every turn becomes a geometric problem — where to break through, how far exploitation can reach before overextending your OWN supply. Reductive design: combat resolution stays simple because the interesting decisions live one layer up.
systems.weaknesses: It's a puzzle game: fixed scenarios, scripted setups, limited replayability — the model has never been proven at continuous grand-strategy scale with production and politics underneath. Supply visibility needs constant overlay-checking. Player-side prestige hoarding showed that scarce consumables get psychologically frozen.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the doctrine wholesale: supply state should be the dominant multiplier in our combat equation — something like full-supply 1.0x vs cut-off 0.3x combat effectiveness plus daily cohesion/strength bleed, so that a division that cuts a rail line accomplishes more than ten divisions grinding frontally. We already simulate rail-era economies and regional power grids; extend that graph to military supply flow per province (capacity-limited rail/port throughput, WitE2-style, but simplified to a flow computation refreshed daily, not hourly, for performance). This is ALSO the answer to how limited war stays interesting: interdiction (air strikes on rail, partisans, naval blockade) manipulates the same supply graph below the escalation ceiling. Korea vertical slice writes itself: Pusan perimeter = supply-rich defender; Inchon = supply-severing landing; Chosin = what being out of supply in winter does. Make the supply overlay a first-class always-available map mode from day one.

systems.domain: Decisive Campaigns: Barbarossa (postures, readiness/fatigue, political-command layer)
systems.how_it_works: Hex-and-counter operational engine with a distinctive stance economy: units hold postures (e.g., Blitzkrieg/Offensive/Defensive); a Soviet division in Offensive vs Defensive posture swings combat value ~60%. Fatigue accumulates only under aggressive postures and suppresses Readiness; Readiness recovers from supply each turn but fatigue knocks it back down — an explicit operational-tempo governor: you physically cannot attack continuously. On top sits an RPG/decision layer where you manage subordinate generals' personalities and field demands from higher command (Hitler's directives), with your standing as a currency.
systems.strengths: Best-in-class model of operational tempo — offensives culminate because the math makes them culminate (fatigue/readiness/supply), which is exactly the anti-WW1-grinding mechanism: attacks come in pulses with regroup phases, like real 20th-century operations. The political layer (arguing with high command, managing prima-donna generals) is beloved and unique.
systems.weaknesses: Turn-based, single-scenario scope, niche UI; the decision layer is heavily hand-authored and doesn't obviously proceduralize. Posture micromanagement per-unit would be tedious at 4,600-province scale.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT both halves. (1) Give armies/theaters (not individual divisions) posture settings and a fatigue↔readiness loop: offensives are launched as operations that spend a preparation/readiness pool and culminate — this converts front-line war from continuous grinding into a rhythm of preparation, offensive pulse, exploitation, culmination, which is dramatically better pacing for RTwP (players plan while paused, watch the pulse execute). (2) The Truman–MacArthur dynamic IS DC:Barbarossa's high-command layer inverted: the player as national leader faces generals demanding escalation (cross the parallel? bomb the bridges? use nukes?) — hand-author this for the Korea slice; it fuses the combat layer to our escalation-ceiling pillar better than any pure mechanic could.

systems.domain: Classic hex-wargame CRTs (odds-ratio table lookup)
systems.how_it_works: Attacker sums attack factors, defender sums defense; compute odds ratio rounded down (1:2, 1:1, 3:1...), roll a d6, cross-index on the Combat Results Table for a result: Attacker Eliminated / Defender Retreat / Exchange / Defender Eliminated, or step losses. Built on the '3:1 rule' maxim. Variants: differential CRTs (attack−defense), step-loss CRTs, low-luck CRTs. Zones of Control pin units and cut retreat paths; many designs add exploitation movement phases for mechanized units after combat (the SPI 'Panzergruppe Guderian' lineage), which is where classic encirclement play comes from.
systems.strengths: Fifty years of refined design wisdom about what results tables must contain: retreats and disruption results (not just losses) are what make lines move; ZOC + retreat-path rules are the original encirclement mechanic (no retreat path = eliminated); exploitation phases prove that breakthrough requires a movement-differential reward, not just a combat win. Fully deterministic-legible: players compute odds before committing.
systems.weaknesses: Odds-rounding creates threshold gaming (shave forces to exactly 3:1); 'soak-off' sacrificial attacks exploit mandatory-attack rules; column results leap discontinuously between odds bands. A CRT is a turn-based artifact — a discrete lookup per attack has no meaning at hourly continuous resolution. Criticism thread ('Death to the CRT') notes tables hide the model instead of expressing it.
systems.lesson_for_1950: AVOID the table, ADOPT the three buried lessons: (1) resolution outputs must include a rich result vocabulary beyond casualties — retreat, disruption (cohesion penalty + can't attack for N hours), shattered — because varied outcomes are what animate a front; (2) retreat-path logic: a unit forced to retreat with no friendly-controlled adjacent province surrenders — this is the encirclement payoff rule, and it must be in from the start; (3) exploitation must be paid in MOVEMENT: after a defender's cohesion collapses, attackers with mobile units should get hours-to-days of unopposed movement before a new line forms (defender re-entrenchment timers) — mechanized/armor value in our unit designer should largely be about who exploits, not who wins the stat trade. That's the entire difference between WW1 grinding and 1950-era maneuver.

systems.domain: Lanchester equations (aggregate attrition math and its pathologies)
systems.how_it_works: Lanchester's Square Law: with ranged fire and full target access, force effectiveness scales with the SQUARE of numbers (dA/dt = −kB, dB/dt = −cA) — two sequential 500-man engagements against 1000 men are catastrophically worse than one 1000 vs 1000 fight. Linear Law (frontage-constrained combat) scales linearly. Used explicitly in RTS combat prediction (StarCraft AI papers) and implicitly in any 'sum stats, trade damage' resolver. Ernest Adams' designer's-notebook piece is the standard games treatment.
systems.strengths: Honest math for aggregate attrition; instantly reveals a design's concentration incentives before you build it. Useful internally as an AI evaluation function (predict battle outcomes for AI theater planning without simulating).
systems.weaknesses: Raw Square Law is the doomstack generator: whoever concentrates more wins superlinearly, so the dominant strategy is always one giant stack — the pathology behind every doomstack meta in 4X/GSG history. It also predicts pure grinding: no breakthrough, no maneuver, just integrals until one side is zero.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT as an analysis tool, AVOID as a resolution model. Concretely: frontage caps per province edge deliberately push our combat toward the LINEAR law (extra divisions beyond the width wait in reserve, adding staying power, not firepower) — this is the mathematical anti-doomstack device and it's why combat width exists in HoI4 at all. Tune reserve rotation so depth still matters (fresh units cycle in as cohesion drops) without superlinear stacking. Separately, run closed-form Lanchester-style estimates as the AI's and the player's battle-forecast tool ('projected: front stabilizes in 6 days, ~12k casualties') — cheap, and it gives the unit designer a testing ground: let players simulate their design against a reference threat before production, Rule the Waves-style, which also guards against RtW3's cardinal sin of unit design that resolution then ignores.

key_takeaways: Architecture verdict: HoI4's skeleton is the only proven fit for RTwP + hourly ticks + thousands of provinces — persistent per-province battle entities, two-track damage (fast-recovering Cohesion decides battles, slow-recovering Strength consumes the economy), frontage caps per edge, and only-active-battles computation. Build that in Bevy ECS and diverge from HoI4 in the surrounding layers, not the core loop.

Deterministic-in-expectation, stochastic-in-texture: with hundreds of hourly resolution events per battle, per-tick variance self-averages, so keep per-hit dice small and put meaningful randomness only at the 12–24h 'tactics draw' layer (general-driven, readable, flavorful). Never let one roll decide a battle (EU4's failure), and never hide the model (AGEOD's failure) — every modifier must be a named, inspectable number, because the unit designer only creates agency if players can predict how a design performs.

Encirclement and maneuver are not combat-math features — they come from three specific mechanisms that must all ship: (1) supply as the dominant combat multiplier with cut-off units bleeding cohesion daily (Unity of Command), (2) retreat-path logic where units with no exit surrender (classic CRT/ZOC rules), (3) exploitation paid in movement — post-breakthrough hours of unopposed advance before defender re-entrenchment timers rebuild the line (SPI exploitation phases). Mechanized units in the unit designer should be valuable mainly for who exploits, not who wins stat trades.

WW1 grinding is prevented by an operational-tempo governor, not by bigger attack numbers: adopt DC:Barbarossa's fatigue↔readiness loop at army/theater level so offensives are prepared, pulse, and culminate — and note that in OUR game residual stalemate is a feature: static grinding fronts are the pressure that tempts players up the escalation ladder, fusing the combat layer to the brinkmanship pillar. Add AGEOD's lesson that weather/supply attrition should rival combat losses (Chosin is the vertical-slice proof case).

Unit design shape: division/brigade templates whose stats aggregate from equipment the existing industry sim produces (closing the steel/oil/factory loop), with logistics footprint (supply tonnage, road/rail dependence, fuel burn) as a first-class design stat so the designer binds to the supply graph. Kill known degenerate metas at the spec stage: no solvable magic-integer frontage, no exploitable weighted-average armor (saturating curves or per-battalion checks), and provide an in-game Lanchester-style battle simulator so players can test designs pre-production — avoiding Rule the Waves 3's sin of elaborate design that resolution ignores.

Limited war needs political friction, not command RNG: replace AGEOD-style activation dice with visible, deterministic constraints — ROE, escalation authorization, coalition caveats ('may not cross the Yalu'), and a hand-authored high-command negotiation layer (the Truman–MacArthur dynamic, straight from DC:Barbarossa's decision system) — so the escalation ceiling is experienced inside the combat layer, not as a separate menu.

systems.domain: HoI4 battle planner and front-line AI
systems.how_it_works: Player draws front lines along borders and offensive lines/arrows into enemy territory; divisions assigned to the order auto-distribute along the front. Stationary divisions with offensive orders accrue a planning bonus (+2%/day base, cap 30%; general planning skill adds +2% cap and +5% accrual per point). Planning decays 1%/day when the AI executes but 3%/day if the player manually moves units — a deliberate incentive to delegate. Execution aggressiveness has three settings (careful/balanced/aggressive). Armies cap at 24 divisions per general (72 on garrison orders); field marshals span armies with front/fallback orders. Spearhead orders advance on a fixed one-province-wide path for armored exploitation. The front-distribution algorithm re-balances divisions continuously as the front geometry changes: when a province is taken or lost the planner recomputes coverage and immediately issues moves, even preemptively so no province is vacant for an hour.
systems.strengths: Genuinely lets one player command 200+ divisions on a 1,000-km front; drawing arrows on a map is intuitive and evocative (the 'crayon plan' is beloved as fantasy fulfillment); the planning-bonus/decay asymmetry is a smart mechanical bribe to stay at high altitude; spearheads give a mid-altitude tool for operational intent without per-unit orders; the planner degrades gracefully — you can grab any division manually at any time, and the handoff is seamless.
systems.weaknesses: The infamous shuffling: every front-geometry change triggers global redistribution, so divisions march laterally along the front instead of holding, burning organization and opening gaps mid-battle; fronts touching multiple countries split/merge unpredictably, orphaning divisions or teleporting assignments; area-defense units abandon posts to chase one landed enemy division. Worse, the meta punishes delegation: manual micro (especially tank micro and encirclements) massively outperforms the planner, so competitive play is 100% micro and the planner is a noob trap — the tool meant to remove micro instead created a skill cliff. AI execution grinds frontal attacks it cannot win, bleeding equipment. Naval-invasion micro cheese bypasses fronts entirely.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT the delegation bribe, AVOID the emergent-geometry frontline object. Two lessons are load-bearing for us: (1) make delegation mechanically superior, not just convenient — HoI4's 3x planning decay for manual moves is the right instinct; in our game, manual province-level meddling should cost command coherence/readiness so posture-level play is the dominant strategy, not the casual crutch; (2) never let the AI re-derive force distribution from live front geometry every tick — that is the root cause of shuffling. Assign forces to STABLE, player-named sectors (e.g. 'I Corps sector: Kaesong–Chorwon') whose boundaries only change when the player redraws them, and let the AI position units within a sector with hysteresis (only move when coverage deficit exceeds a threshold for N hours). With hourly ticks and 4,600 provinces, tick-reactive rebalancing would be shuffling hell; sector-stability plus damped repositioning kills the bug class outright.

systems.domain: Victoria 3 fronts and generals
systems.how_it_works: Armies are formations of standardized battalions raised from barracks buildings; the player never touches the map. A 'front' is an auto-generated object spawning wherever two belligerents' states touch. The player assigns generals to fronts and sets a strategy: advance or defend (originally per-general orders like 'Attack' with weekly battle rolls). Battles are abstracted: the sim picks a battle location, draws N battalions per side based on general rank and front width, rolls combat with modifiers, and the winner flips some provinces. Paradox's stated intent (DD#23): war is an extension of diplomacy in an economy game; account for every serviceman in the pop simulation while giving only 'a high-level strategic interface to monitor and manipulate'; they explicitly resisted controls that would let players micro generals' moment-to-moment priorities. Patches 1.5–1.9 added formation-based armies, mobilization option customization, and front-advance visualizations without changing the core.
systems.strengths: The intent is exactly right for a limited-war game: war as resource competition decided by industry, logistics, manpower, and tech rather than tactical cleverness; zero unit micro at any scale; casualties feed straight back into the pop/economy sim; wars stay playable unpaused at full speed. Worth stealing conceptually even though execution failed.
systems.weaknesses: The most-criticized war system in recent memory, and the failures are specific: (1) fronts are emergent objects, so when geometry changes (a state flips, an ally joins, a front splits) the front object is destroyed and recreated — assigned generals teleport home and armies vanish mid-war, which is both a bug factory and a micro tax (the system managed to be non-interactive AND micro-heavy); (2) no meaningful player decisions between declaring war and peace — advance/defend is a coin with two faces, so players watch a progress bar they can barely influence; (3) no spatial intent: you cannot prioritize defending a specific city, cannot choose an axis of advance, cannot mass force at a point — the 'barbershop pole' front crawls arbitrarily; (4) opacity: battle resolution (why 40 of my 100 battalions showed up) is illegible, so losses feel random rather than earned; (5) degenerate meta: stack generals on one front, spam biggest formation, win by GDP — which is thematically correct but experientially hollow because the player contributed no decisions.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the philosophy, AVOID the implementation wholesale. V3 proves abstraction is not the sin — decisionlessness and instability are. Three hard rules for us: (1) any object the player assigns forces to must be player-created and persistent, never derived from live map state (this is the same root cause as HoI4 shuffling, and V3 is the cautionary maximum); (2) 'posture over maneuver' still requires 3–6 meaningful knobs per theater — axis/objective selection, force allocation between sectors, posture (dig in / probe / limited offensive / general offensive), escalation ceiling compliance, reserve commitment — each with legible tradeoffs; (3) every battle result must be auditable: show which units engaged, why, and which modifiers decided it. For our Korea slice: the player should be able to say 'hold the Pusan perimeter, prioritize the Naktong crossings, land at Inchon' — V3 can express none of those sentences, and that is precisely why it failed.

systems.domain: Supreme Ruler auto-managed theaters and ministers
systems.how_it_works: Real-time engine on a hex map with thousands of units. The player can delegate per-department to cabinet ministers, and per-unit or globally toggle 'initiative' — units with initiative are moved by the military AI within battle zones/theaters the AI derives from hotspots; sliders set defensive/offensive stance and priorities (e.g. 'maximize active units'). Everything from research to unit deployment can be auto-managed or manually overridden at any grain, down to individual battalions. SR2030 continues the same model.
systems.strengths: The ambition is our ambition: a strategic-scale game where you set policy and the machine fights. Full-spectrum optional delegation (any unit, any department, any time) is the right shape on paper; per-unit initiative flags are a nice granular handoff primitive.
systems.weaknesses: The canonical failure of delegation-by-option rather than delegation-by-design: the minister AI is widely described as 'rather useless' — units with initiative wander out of defensive lines, abandon entrenchment, leave holes, and die pointlessly, so experienced players turn ALL automation off and drown in micro (players report manually driving multi-front wars unit by unit); the hotspot/battle-zone system is erratic and buggy with terrible UI; minister policies have near-zero feedback (GameSpot: cabinet system 'an absolute mess'). Because manual control is always available and the AI is untrustworthy, the game silently becomes a micro game with worse tools than an RTS.
systems.lesson_for_1950: AVOID the architecture, heed the warning. Supreme Ruler proves that if delegation is optional and the AI is even slightly untrustworthy, players ratchet down to manual control and never come back — trust, once lost to one entrenchment-abandoning blunder, is unrecoverable. Consequences for us: (1) do not ship a manual per-unit movement layer as the fallback; make the lowest player altitude the operational directive, so there is no micro floor to fall to and AI quality is a hard launch requirement, not a nice-to-have; (2) AI execution must be conservative by default — holding entrenched positions must be the AI's overwhelming prior, and it should refuse orders it cannot execute with a legible 'why' rather than attempt and bleed; (3) every delegated decision needs feedback ('7th Division withdrew from hill 983: flanked, supply < 40%'). An untrusted subordinate is worse than no subordinate.

systems.domain: HoI3 OOB and chain-of-command delegation
systems.how_it_works: Full hierarchical OOB: division → corps (bonus from leader skill) → army → army group (each leader level cuts supply/fuel use of everything beneath) → theatre HQ. Any HQ at any level can be flagged AI-controlled ('green-flagged') with stance (defensive/offensive/blitz) and objectives; the theatre AI does strategic threat assessment and distributes forces among subordinate commands, or lower HQs can be delegated individually while the player retains theatre control. Radio range/command distance matters. Players developed a whole meta of drawing theatre boundaries narrowly and detaching the theatre AI so corps-level AIs 'focus solely on their objectives' without the top-level threat model overriding them.
systems.strengths: The only Paradox system where delegation altitude was truly player-selectable per formation — command Army Group A personally while Theatre B runs itself is exactly the fantasy; the hierarchy carried mechanical meaning (leader skills, supply efficiency, command range), so OOB design was itself a strategy layer; objectives + stance is a decent directive vocabulary; scoped well, the corps AI was genuinely competent.
systems.weaknesses: Crushing setup burden — hours of drag-and-drop OOB surgery at game start before playing (Paradox explicitly abandoned it for HoI4 partly for this reason); the theatre AI's threat assessment diverged from player intent and had 'AI panic attacks,' yanking forces to phantom threats — the top of the hierarchy was the least trustworthy layer; opaque delegation state (which flag on which HQ does what) with weak UI; the interaction between levels was undocumented folklore.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT — this is our closest ancestor, fixed at the top and bottom. Adopt: a real chain of command (Theater → Army/Corps → auto-managed below) where the player picks their altitude per formation, and where OOB structure has mechanical teeth (commander traits, staff capacity, communications) — for 1950 this is period-perfect: MacArthur's Far East Command, corps commanders with personalities, political generals. Fix: (1) ship pre-built historical OOBs with light editing, never blank-slate assembly — the player customizes, doesn't construct; (2) do NOT give the top-level AI independent strategic judgment that can override player directives — the theater AI allocates within player-set objectives and never invents its own threats; strategic surprise should arrive as intelligence reports demanding a player decision, not as the AI unilaterally redeploying; (3) delegation state must be one glance readable on the map. Commander skill as the delegation-quality dial (a skill-2 corps commander executes your directive sloppily; Ridgway executes it brilliantly) also elegantly ties the espionage/politics layer into war.

systems.domain: AGEOD army postures and WEGO orders
systems.how_it_works: Regional (not province-grid) map, simultaneous-resolution turns of 15 days–1 month. The player never fights battles: each stack gets a posture — offensive (red), defensive (blue), passive (green) — plus rules of engagement (all-out attack … retreat if engaged), and the engine resolves movement, interception, and combat simultaneously for both sides. Supporting mechanics: march-to-the-sound-of-guns (nearby friendly stacks with the right posture/commander auto-reinforce battles), command-point penalties for stacks led by insufficient-rank commanders, leader activation rolls (a dithering general may simply not move this turn), cohesion/supply attrition dominating casualties, and 400+ rated historical leaders whose traits gate what their formations will actually do.
systems.strengths: The purest existing statement of 'posture over maneuver': intent + tolerance, then commit and watch — decisions feel like command, not piloting; WEGO forces anticipation of enemy movement rather than reaction, which reads as genuine operational art; leader activation and command-point rules make the OOB and personalities the real game; postures + ROE is a compact, legible directive vocabulary (two dials express most of operational intent); attrition-dominant combat suits limited war.
systems.weaknesses: Brutal learning curve and manual-dependency (logistics folklore required or you lose to attrition invisibly); resolution opacity — turns resolve with weak playback, so players often can't tell why a battle happened or didn't; the engine's interception/MTSG logic misfires enough that veterans build elaborate superstitions around it; pacing is wrong for anything but its niche (a 15–30 day commit is far too coarse for a crisis game); passive-posture exploits and activation-roll fishing exist as minor metas.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the posture+ROE vocabulary as our core directive grammar — it is the best fit in the genre for escalation-ceiling warfare. Concretely: each theater force gets a posture (entrench / screen / probe / limited offensive / general offensive) crossed with an ROE that we bind directly to the escalation system (weapons release authority, cross-border pursuit, air interdiction depth, proximity to superpower forces) — 'hold the parallel, do not pursue north, no air strikes within 50km of the Yalu' becomes a literal order, and ROE violations by aggressive commanders become escalation incidents, which turns AGEOD's leader-personality friction into brinkmanship gameplay. Also adopt leader activation/friction: real-time-with-pause plus hourly ticks gives us continuous WEGO for free — orders take hours to propagate down the chain and days to take effect, which naturally creates AGEOD's commit-and-anticipate feel without discrete turns. Avoid its opacity: we need an after-action layer (why this battle, who reinforced, what the ROE prevented) as a first-class UI.

systems.domain: Unit design (HoI4 division designer) and its interface to delegated command
systems.how_it_works: HoI4's division designer: templates built from battalions and support companies on a 5-column grid, costing army XP per change; stats (soft attack, breakthrough, org, width) derive from composition; equipment variants designed separately (tank/plane designers with modules). All fielded divisions of a template update when it changes. The designer coexists with the battle planner: players design templates, the planner fields and fights them. Community meta: template optimization is a beloved deep endgame (widths, 40w meta pre-Barbarossa patch, space marines) but also a wiki-dependency and exploit surface.
systems.strengths: The single most-loved system in HoI4 and the proof our director's hard requirement is compatible with delegated command: unit DESIGN is a paused, deliberate, industrial-strategic act, entirely orthogonal to unit DRIVING. It creates identity ('my Korea infantry template'), consumes economic output meaningfully, and rewards doctrine thinking. Template-wide retrofit ties design to industry.
systems.weaknesses: Solved-meta problem: one optimal template per role emerges and is copied from wikis, deleting the design space; exploits (space marines) come from unconstrained mixing; stat soup is illegible to new players; nothing ties a design to the command layer — the AI fights a bad template exactly as confidently as a good one, with no feedback loop from front performance to design.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT enthusiastically — this is where the director's requirement lives, and it slots perfectly under high-altitude command. Player designs at two levels: equipment (a 1950s MBT: gun/armor/engine/electronics trading steel, industrial capacity, and fuel draw against our existing resource sim) and formation templates (a US infantry division vs. a Soviet mechanized division: battalion mix, support, motorization — consuming our demographic cohorts and military-industrial allocation directly). Then the COMMAND layer fields templates: the player decides WHAT the army is made of and WHERE/HOW HARD it fights; the AI decides which province each formation stands in. Anti-meta measures: doctrine/national trees that fork the design space so US and Soviet optima differ; intelligence-limited knowledge of enemy designs (espionage reveals the T-54's armor basis — ties in our espionage pillar); and close the loop AGEOD/HoI4 never did — after-action reports flag design deficiencies ('our tanks are outranged', historical rhyme: Task Force Smith's bazookas bouncing off T-34s), making redesign a narrative beat.

key_takeaways: The genre's two catastrophic failures (HoI4 shuffling, V3 vanishing fronts) share ONE root cause: forces assigned to emergent objects derived from live map geometry. Rule zero for us: players assign forces to player-created, persistent objects (named theaters/sectors with player-drawn boundaries), and the AI repositions within them with hysteresis — never tick-reactive rebalancing.

Command altitude answer: the player operates at theater/operational-directive level — named sectors, posture x ROE, axis/objective selection, reserve commitment, and force allocation — while the AI executes all province-level positioning and combat. Critically (Supreme Ruler's lesson), do NOT ship a per-unit manual layer as a fallback: if micro exists and the AI is imperfect, players ratchet down to micro and delegation dies. The directive layer must be the floor, which makes conservative, legible AI execution a launch-blocking requirement.

Victoria 3 proves abstraction is not the sin — decisionlessness and opacity are. Between declaring war and peace the player needs 3-6 meaningful, spatial, legible decisions per theater ('hold Pusan, prioritize the Naktong, land at Inchon'), and every battle result must be auditable (who fought, why there, what modifier decided it). An after-action/'why' layer is first-class UI, not polish.

AGEOD's posture+ROE vocabulary is the best existing grammar for limited war under escalation ceilings — and ROE should be literally bound to our escalation system (pursuit limits, weapons release, interdiction depth near superpower forces). Aggressive commanders violating ROE become escalation incidents, converting command friction into brinkmanship gameplay; real-time-with-pause + hourly ticks + order-propagation delay gives us WEGO's commit-and-anticipate feel continuously for free.

The unit-design hard requirement is not in tension with high-altitude command — HoI4 proves they're orthogonal and synergistic: design (equipment + formation templates) is a paused industrial-strategic act consuming our existing steel/oil/cohort/industry sim; command fields the results. Player decides WHAT the army is and WHERE/HOW HARD it fights; AI decides which province each unit stands in. Fight solved-meta with doctrine-forked design spaces and espionage-gated knowledge of enemy designs.
