Make delegation mechanically superior, not merely convenient (HoI4's 3x planning-decay for manual moves is the right instinct — ours: manual meddling costs command coherence/readiness), pre-build historical OOBs rather than HoI3's blank-slate assembly, give the chain of command mechanical teeth via commander skill/traits as the delegation-quality dial, and never give top-level AI independent strategic judgment that overrides player directives — HoI3's 'AI panic attacks' killed trust exactly as SR's minister blunders did.

reports.games: Surveyed in depth: The Korean War (Victory Games/Balkoski 1986), Next War: Korea (GMT), Twilight Struggle (GMT), Fire in the Lake (GMT COIN), Vietnam '65 (Every Single Soldier), Hearts of Iron IV + Conditional Surrender/volunteer mechanics + designers (tank/plane/ship/division), Victoria 3 (diplomatic plays), Rule the Waves 2/3 (NWS/Slitherine), Shadow Empire (VR Designs), Flashpoint Campaigns: Red Storm/Southern Storm, Wargame: Red Dragon (Second Korean War campaign) / WARNO, DEFCON (Introversion), ICBM: Escalation, Command: Modern Operations (ROE/doctrine), Sea Power, Supreme Ruler: Cold War, Terminal Conflict, East vs. West (cancelled Paradox title), The Operational Art of War (Korea scenarios), Twilight: 2000 (GDW setting + Last Battle), EU4 warscore/peace system as genre baseline.

systems.domain: Escalation ceilings and DEFCON-style tracks
systems.how_it_works: Twilight Struggle: a 5-step DEFCON track; coups in battlegrounds degrade DEFCON; at DEFCON 2 whole classes of actions become 'suicide cards' (whoever triggers DEFCON 1 instantly loses); play naturally equilibrates at DEFCON 2 nearly all game. It also has Required Military Operations: each turn you must spend ops on military actions equal to the DEFCON level or lose VP — domestic hawks punish pure dovishness. Next War: Korea gates nuclear/chemical release and third-party entry behind advanced-rules political checks. ICBM: Escalation's Standoff mode explicitly stages conventional skirmish → limited exchange → full nuclear war. DEFCON (Introversion) makes everyone lose (score = fewest civilian deaths, default 2 pts/kill, -1/loss) — MAD as chicken. East vs West planned DEFCON levels + a Doomsday Clock gating unit behavior.
systems.strengths: Twilight Struggle's is the single best-proven design: the ceiling is a shared, visible resource both sides manipulate, and 'who is holding the escalation hot potato when it drops' creates constant brinkmanship without simulating nuclear war at all. Instant-loss for the escalator makes restraint self-enforcing. Required Military Ops elegantly forces limited wars to exist.
systems.weaknesses: In TS the track degenerates to 'park at DEFCON 2 forever' — tension becomes static background, not a crisis. Instant-loss rules feel arbitrary in a videogame with more state than a card game. DEFCON-the-game shows pure MAD scoring makes the pre-nuclear phase perfunctory. ICBM reviews note conventional war is a shallow prelude to the nukes.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT a visible, mutual escalation ladder as THE core war container, but make it per-conflict (a Korea theater has its own escalation level nested under global DEFCON), and make the ceiling define legal actions: at each rung, specific target sets, weapon classes, and geography unlock. Avoid the static-DEFCON-2 degeneracy by making each rung decay toward peace unless fed (crises spike it, time and diplomacy lower it) and by pricing rungs asymmetrically per superpower per theater. Total war = someone rode the ladder off the top; that's your failure state, so the top rung should transfer catastrophic, visible costs BEFORE the nukes fly (mobilization wrecking the civilian economy your sim already models). Adopt a Required-Military-Ops analog: hawkish domestic factions demand visible action, so players can't sit at zero commitment for free.

systems.domain: Rules of engagement and sanctuary borders (no bombing across the Yalu)
systems.how_it_works: Victory Games' The Korean War (1986) is the gold standard: on turn 2 the UN player picks Intervention Level, Mobilization Level, and Rules of Engagement — the ROE choice literally defines which map zones may be bombed and whether atomic use is authorized, and higher settings raise a global Tension track (Tension 7 = Communists win instantly; UN also loses 5×Tension VP per turn). Historically the Manchurian sanctuary let MiGs climb over the Yalu, engage, and dive home; UN pursuit was forbidden. Command: Modern Operations models this as per-side/per-mission ROE and doctrine settings plus scenario scoring penalties for striking prohibited targets — the AI obeys ROE, and violating it costs points rather than being hard-blocked in some scenarios.
systems.strengths: Making ROE a chosen policy with a tension price is brilliant: the player self-imposes the historical constraints because escalation is priced, not scripted. Sanctuaries create authentic operational texture (MiG Alley exists BECAUSE of the rule) and interesting asymmetric gameplay — one side's staging areas are inviolable.
systems.weaknesses: Hard-scripted sanctuaries feel like invisible walls if the player can't ever choose to violate them. In CMANO, soft point-penalties let players 'eat the penalty' when the math favors it, which trivializes the politics if the price is only score. Also, only sophisticated players enjoy fighting deliberately hobbled.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT as a first-class 'Theater ROE' policy panel per limited war: target-category and geographic permissions (bomb north of 38th? interdict across Yalu? naval blockade? hot pursuit?) each tied to a rung of the theater escalation level. Violating your declared ROE should be POSSIBLE (order the strike anyway) but should be an escalation event with automatic consequences — enemy patron response, world opinion, domestic politics — resolved by your influence/espionage systems, not a mere score deduction. Sanctuary status should be something the OTHER side's patron confers (Chinese airfields are sanctuaries because China isn't formally at war), which links ROE directly to the intervention-tripwire system. This is cheap to implement on 4,600 provinces: tag province sets as ROE zones.

systems.domain: Proxy, volunteer, and deniable forces (Chinese People's Volunteers, Soviet pilots)
systems.how_it_works: HOI4: 'send volunteers' lets a non-belligerent commit capped forces — 1 division per 20 you own, also capped by target's size (≈7 divisions max into Spain), air volunteers 1 wing per 500 planes; sending them raises World Tension proportional to size; democracies need 50% tension to send any. Volunteers fight under your control with your equipment but no war declaration. Victory Games' Korean War models Chinese intervention at two discrete levels (limited vs full), plus optional Soviet and Nationalist Chinese entry. Twilight Struggle abstracts all proxy war into coups/realignments — influence warfare with military ops flavor. Historically, Soviet pilots flew in Korea under deniability constraints (no flying over water, no English on radio) — no game models the deniability-maintenance itself well.
systems.strengths: HOI4's cap formula is a decent 'commitment ≠ belligerency' template, and tension-cost-proportional-to-size is the right price structure. Volunteers under sender control give the proxy patron real gameplay, not a spectator role.
systems.weaknesses: In HOI4 volunteers are a free farm: XP, army experience, and zero diplomatic risk beyond tension — the fiction of deniability is never testable, never blown. No game makes the DENIABILITY itself a resource that intelligence can strip away. Discrete two-level intervention (limited/full) is authentic but AI-opaque in digital implementations.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT and go further: make deniability a stat. Committed foreign forces carry a cover level (volunteers, advisors, 'technicians') degraded by scale, casualties, POWs, and enemy espionage; your espionage pillar gets a concrete job — proving Soviet pilots are flying MiGs — and PROVEN involvement is what triggers escalation/tripwire consequences, while suspected involvement only moves opinion. Cap deniable commitment by type and scale HOI4-style (air and advisors cheap to hide, armor and formations expensive). This is the mechanic that makes Korea-as-vertical-slice sing: China can enter as 'People's Volunteers' at a lower escalation rung than open war, exactly as happened.

systems.domain: Intervention tripwires and third-party entry
systems.how_it_works: Next War: Korea: while any Allied unit is north of the DMZ (non-DMZ hex), a die is rolled each UN-Resolution segment; China intervenes on 0 or less, with modifiers — a transparent, probabilistic tripwire keyed to a geographic line. Victory Games' Korean War ties intervention scale/timing to UN choices (crossing the 38th, approaching the Yalu). HOI4 uses guarantees/factions plus world-tension thresholds unlocking AI behaviors. Supreme Ruler: Cold War is the cautionary tale: its AI simply never intervenes in Korea/Vietnam, making them 'predictable and boring' per reviews.
systems.strengths: Geographic tripwires with visible odds create the authentic MacArthur dilemma: every hex north of a line is a gamble the player chooses with open eyes. Probabilistic beats deterministic — you can't perfectly game it, but you can price it.
systems.weaknesses: Fully hidden thresholds (Supreme Ruler) read as AI passivity or arbitrary betrayal. Fully known deterministic lines get min-maxed (advance exactly to the line and stop). Die-roll-per-turn systems can produce absurd outcomes (China shrugs as you occupy Pyongyang for a year) without escalating modifiers.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT probabilistic tripwires with PARTIALLY visible risk: the player sees an intelligence ESTIMATE of intervention risk (espionage quality determines estimate accuracy — your spy pillar again), while the true hazard function keys off objective triggers: provinces held past declared lines, proximity to patron borders, strikes on patron assets, ROE violations, and cumulative time. Make risk cumulative and rising, not memoryless per-tick. Crucially, intervention should usually arrive as deniable/volunteer forces first (previous domain), giving a graduated response instead of a lightswitch to WW3. Publish some red lines diplomatically (patrons can declare them), so the map has legible political geography.

systems.domain: Ending wars short of total victory: armistice, stalemate, negotiated peace
systems.how_it_works: Genre baseline (EU4): warscore 0-100 from battles/occupation/objectives, spent on a peace-deal shopping list; wars routinely end partial. HOI4: wars end ONLY in capitulation-and-conference — universally criticized ('march through every enemy capital to take the Falklands'); huge mods (Conditional Surrender, Make Peace Not War) exist solely to fix it via event-chain peace offers keyed to surrender progress and war support. Victoria 3 diplomatic plays: three outcomes (you back down, they back down, war), and community consensus is it funnels everything into world wars; backing down ≈ conceding without a fight. Rule the Waves: wars end by negotiation driven by accumulating VP, war-duration weariness, and blockade status — you can WIN a war after losing battles if prestige holds; peace terms transfer bases/colonies, then the game continues into the interwar buildup, which is where its heart is. Fire in the Lake: game ends at a final coup card; if nobody met their victory threshold, closest-to-threshold wins — stalemate is scored, not extended. Victory Games' Korean War: UN chooses between political victory (VP, penalized 5×Tension/turn) or military conquest; the historical armistice emerges as the rational choice under tension pressure.
systems.strengths: Warscore-style systems prove partial peace is mechanically easy. RTW proves the best version: because the GAME is the long competition, an individual war is a round you can afford to end — wars end when both sides' continuing costs exceed expected gains, which is the actual theory of war termination. Fire in the Lake proves 'closest to objectives at the whistle' makes stalemate a real, scored outcome.
systems.weaknesses: Warscore degenerates into 'farm score, cash out' — peace as vending machine, and AI acceptance math gets gamed. HOI4 shows the cost of NOT having this: every border skirmish becomes total war, which is precisely your declared failure state. Vic3 shows that if backing down is pure loss, nobody backs down and everything escalates. Ceasefire timers without a line-based settlement produce forever-frozen fronts with no closure.
systems.lesson_for_1950: This is the highest-stakes system for your game: ADOPT armistice-along-the-line-of-control as the DEFAULT war ending. Model each limited war with per-side war objectives and a negotiation state: at any time either side can propose armistice; acceptance is driven by front-line position vs objectives, cumulative casualties/cost, patron pressure (superpowers can force clients to the table — your influence pillar), and domestic weariness. Korea's endgame — two years of talks while fighting continues over the final line — suggests a killer mechanic: once talks open, every province taken is a bargaining chip, and fighting-while-negotiating has its own escalation etiquette. Absolutely AVOID HOI4's capitulation-only model, and avoid Vic3's back-down-is-total-humiliation by making partial climbdowns purchasable (concede one objective, keep another). The armistice should leave persistent world-state: DMZs, frozen conflicts, divided states — fuel for the next 40 years of Cold War.

systems.domain: War weariness and domestic politics as the throttle on war
systems.how_it_works: Vietnam '65: two currencies — Political Points (Washington's patience; every reinforcement costs more than the last; earned by kills, spent on everything) and Hearts & Minds (the actual victory metric, earned by presence and security, not combat). Fire in the Lake: US victory = total Support + US troops/bases OUT of country (in the Available box) ≥ 50 — you must win AND go home; casualties move pieces to out-of-play, wrecking this. Victory Games' Korean War: -5 VP × Tension per turn makes escalation corrosively expensive over time. Victoria 3/HOI4: war support/stability sliders drained by casualties/attrition, modified by ideology. Rule the Waves: naval budget is set by parliament, swings with tension and prestige; losing prestige constrains you more than losing ships.
systems.strengths: Vietnam '65's escalating-cost-per-reinforcement is the cleanest 'limited commitment' mechanic ever shipped — Washington's reluctance is priced into every requisition. Fire in the Lake's 'victory includes withdrawal' is the deepest single insight: for a democracy in a limited war, the win condition itself contains the exit. These make restraint strategic rather than moralizing.
systems.weaknesses: Simple weariness sliders (Civ/EU4/HOI4) are just a countdown clock — players treat them as a timer to race, and they're trivially patched by modifiers. If weariness only ever rises, the optimal play is always blitz, which fights your real-time 41-year structure. Politics-as-slider also misses WHO objects: no factions, no elections, no MacArthur-vs-Truman.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT aggressively: you already simulate demographic cohorts per province — casualties should come FROM specific cohorts and provinces, so war weariness is emergent and geographic (draft riots where the dead come from), not a global slider. Give each superpower a domestic-politics layer with hawks and doves whose strength shifts with casualties, atrocity/escalation events, and election cycles (US elections every 2/4 years are natural escalation/de-escalation clocks; 1952 'I shall go to Korea' should be modelable). Commitment ceilings, not just weariness: Congress/Politburo authorizes force levels and budgets per theater, Vietnam-'65-style with escalating marginal cost. For the USSR, weariness manifests differently — elite politics and economic strain rather than opinion polls — which showcases your systems-competition pillar.

systems.domain: Player-designed units under period constraints (the hard requirement)
systems.how_it_works: Three proven templates. HOI4: chassis + module slots (tank: chassis, armament, turret, 4 specials; plane: airframe, mandatory engine, special modules with weight/reliability/cost tradeoffs), plus a separate division designer (combine battalions into templates); stats emerge from modules. Rule the Waves: freeform ship design under hard constraints — displacement, budget, dock size, build-tonnage caps, and TREATY LIMITS (Washington-style tonnage/gun caps you negotiate); designs take years to build, so you're betting on the future threat environment; ships age, doctrine and tech shift value. Shadow Empire: parametric model design (pick gun, engine, armor; stats derive from physics-ish formulas) feeding an OOB of formation templates.
systems.strengths: HOI4's designers are beloved and drive enormous engagement/DLC value — module tinkering is intrinsically fun and mods prove appetite for more. RTW's genius is that design is embedded in the PEACETIME competition: you design under uncertainty about the war you'll actually fight, under budgets and treaties, and live with 20-year-old hulls — perfect Cold War texture (MiG-15 vs Sabre, missile-vs-gun bets, 'bomber gap' guesswork). Shadow Empire shows derived-stat design stays coherent.
systems.weaknesses: HOI4's meta degenerated notoriously: 'cardboard tanks' and 'land battleships' (min-maxed absurd designs) because stats are additive and combat model exploitable; designers also add busywork — players copy internet templates, and the AI designs badly, so player advantage compounds. RTW design UI is spreadsheet-hostile. Any designer multiplies balance surface area.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the RTW frame with HOI4's module UX: unit design is primarily a PEACETIME arms-race activity — design the MiG-17 answer to the Sabre, the T-54 line, under budget, doctrine, and (later) arms-control treaty constraints, with multi-year lead times so espionage (stealing the other side's design specs — your pillar!) and intelligence estimates of enemy designs matter enormously. Tie designs to your existing industry sim: a design consumes specific steel/oil/electronics and specific factory retooling, so 'cardboard tank' cheese dies naturally — the constraint system, not stat caps, prevents degenerate designs. Design at the equipment level (tank/aircraft/ship classes) plus a division/regiment template layer for force structure; limited wars then become live-fire testbeds where your export clients and volunteers fly your designs and reveal their flaws (Korea as the F-86/MiG-15 proving ground). Make the AI use a curated design library so it stays competitive.

systems.domain: Operational conduct of limited war: command friction and force pools (Cold-War-gone-hot games)
systems.how_it_works: Flashpoint Campaigns Red Storm/Southern Storm: asymmetric OODA-loop turns — your order cycle might be 30+ minutes of game time while a better-C3 enemy cycles every 13; you issue intent, then watch friction, EW, and subordinate initiative play out; regarded as the best 'WW3 1989' operational game. Wargame: Red Dragon's Second Korean War campaign: battlegroups drawn from a finite force pool maneuver on a strategic map; Political Points buy reinforcements; Cohesion (morale) both gates battle initiative and is the campaign resource — you win campaigns by breaking enemy cohesion/morale, not annihilation. Twilight: 2000 (1984 GDW RPG): the WW3 setting where a LIMITED nuclear exchange happened and everything broke — its enduring lesson is aesthetic: WW3 is depicted exclusively as aftermath and ruin, never as a fun war to win. CMOA/Sea Power cover the tactical missile-age layer.
systems.strengths: Flashpoint proves command friction IS the Cold War operational experience — C3/EW as first-class stats differentiates the superpowers' doctrines beautifully. Wargame's finite force pool + cohesion-victory is exactly how a limited war should feel: you fight with what the politicians gave you, and wars end when armies are exhausted, not annihilated. Twilight 2000's framing reinforces your design thesis: the actual WW3 is only compelling as a horror/failure state.
systems.weaknesses: Deep command friction frustrates mainstream players (top Red Storm forum thread: 'why don't my units move?'). Wargame's campaign AI and stack-of-doom issues; RTS-layer skill dominating strategy-layer decisions. None of these connect the operational layer back to politics — the ceiling is scenario-fixed, not player-negotiated.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT the force-pool concept as the bridge between your domestic-politics throttle and the front line: a theater command receives authorized formations, air sorties, and supply flow set by the political layer; the theater fights RTS-with-pause at hourly ticks with modest command friction (order delays scaled by C3 doctrine — a real US-vs-Soviet differentiator and an espionage target). Victory at the theater level should be cohesion/position-based (feeding the armistice negotiation state), never annihilation-based. Keep friction light-touch — delayed order execution and imperfect intel, not Flashpoint-grade opacity. AVOID making the operational layer skill-dominant over the political layer; the interesting decisions are what to ask Washington/Moscow for, and what the front's state does to the negotiating table.

systems.domain: Whole-Cold-War strategy layers: cautionary post-mortems
systems.how_it_works: Supreme Ruler: Cold War (2011): full 1949+ sim with sphere-of-influence points; reviews and forums document opaque 'invisible equation' mechanics, sphere system that 'does nothing but make nations hate each other,' and an AI that never intervenes in Korea or Vietnam. East vs. West (Paradox, cancelled 2014): HOI3-engine Cold War with DEFCON, Doomsday Clock, spy cards, ICBMs — cancelled after severe delays; the post-mortem consensus is that bolting Cold War politics onto a total-war engine (HOI) failed because the engine's verbs are all about fighting WW3, and 41 years of not-fighting had no gameplay. Terminal Conflict shipped a narrower card/DEFCON hybrid to a niche audience. Twilight Struggle remains the only mass-loved full-Cold-War game — and it contains no conventional warfare at all.
systems.strengths: These establish the field's negative space clearly and cheaply.
systems.weaknesses: Supreme Ruler: opacity kills — if intervention logic and influence math are invisible, players experience arbitrary AI, and the Cold War reads as either dead calm or random WW3. East vs West: the engine's core loop must BE the cold competition, not a wargame idling for decades. Twilight Struggle's success without any conventional war shows the war layer must justify itself — which your unit-design + limited-war requirement can do only if wars are frequent enough (Korea, Suez, Vietnam, Indo-Pak, Middle East) and consequential to the influence game.
systems.lesson_for_1950: AVOID both failure modes by inverting East vs West: build the game as an influence/economy/espionage engine (which you have) where limited wars are high-stakes EPISODES with clear entry (crisis escalation), conduct (theater ROE + force pools), and exit (armistice machinery) — each war changing the influence map, testing player-designed hardware, and feeding the arms race. Make all political math legible: show intervention-risk estimates, tension sources, and weariness drivers on-screen. The 41-year structure needs a steady drumbeat of client-state wars (roughly one active crisis/proxy war at most times, historically accurate) so the unit-design and war systems are exercised continuously without the player's OWN superpower being at war more than rarely.

key_takeaways: Wars must end at the line of control, not at capitulation. HOI4's capitulation-only model is the genre's most-modded-out failure and is fatal to a limited-war game; build the armistice as a first-class negotiation state (front position vs war objectives + casualties + patron pressure + domestic weariness) where fighting-during-talks turns provinces into bargaining chips, and where partial climbdowns are purchasable so backing down isn't Vic3-style total humiliation. The resulting DMZs and frozen conflicts become persistent world-state fueling the next crisis.

Put the escalation ceiling inside the war, and price it, don't script it. Victory Games' Korean War (1986) already solved this: the player CHOOSES intervention level, mobilization, and ROE (bombing zones, atomic release) and pays a tension price per turn for aggressive settings (Tension 7 = instant loss; -5 VP x Tension). Combine that with Next War: Korea's transparent probabilistic tripwire (roll for Chinese entry while units are north of a line) but show the player only an espionage-quality ESTIMATE of the true intervention risk — this turns your spy pillar into the limited-war UI.

Make deniability a stat and proxies a graduated intervention. No shipped game models what made Korea Korea: Chinese 'volunteers' and Soviet pilots entering below the threshold of open war. Adapt HOI4's volunteer caps and tension costs, then add a cover level per foreign contingent that enemy espionage can strip; PROVEN involvement escalates, suspected involvement only shifts opinion. Patron intervention should arrive deniably first — a graduated response ladder instead of a lightswitch to WW3.

Satisfy the unit-design requirement with the Rule the Waves frame, not the HOI4 combat-stat frame: design is a PEACETIME arms-race activity under budget, industry, and treaty constraints, with multi-year lead times, uncertainty about enemy designs (espionage target), and limited wars as live-fire testbeds where clients and volunteers fly your designs (Korea = MiG-15 vs F-86 proving ground). Ground design costs in the existing steel/oil/industry sim so degenerate 'cardboard tank' metas die of resource physics rather than stat caps; give the AI a curated design library.

War weariness should be emergent from the systems you already have, and the throttle should be commitment ceilings, not a slider: casualties drawn from specific demographic cohorts in specific provinces create geographic, faction-mediated domestic politics, while Vietnam '65's escalating marginal cost per reinforcement and Fire in the Lake's 'victory requires bringing the troops home' define how a democracy's limited war should actually feel. US election cycles are natural escalation clocks; Soviet 'weariness' should run through elite politics and economic strain instead — showcasing the systems-competition pillar.

The cautionary post-mortems (Supreme Ruler: Cold War, East vs West) agree: opacity and a total-war engine idling for 40 years both kill the game. Keep every political number legible on-screen (tension sources, intervention estimates, weariness drivers), make the cold competition the core loop, and structure limited wars as recurring, bounded episodes — entry via crisis escalation, conduct via theater ROE + politically-authorized force pools with light command friction, exit via armistice — each one reshaping the influence map and stress-testing the arms race.

reports.games: Hearts of Iron IV: No Step Back (Paradox, 2021); Unity of Command 1 & 2 (2x2 Games, 2011/2019); Gary Grigsby's War in the East 2 (2by3/Matrix, 2021); Supreme Ruler series (BattleGoat, 2005-2014); AGEOD engine titles (Civil War II, To End All Wars, WarPlan-adjacent Athena engine games). Sources: HoI4 Paradox wiki + PCGamesN/EIP supply guides + Paradox forum post-NSB criticism threads; UoC dev diaries ("The Power of Supply" I & II, "The Supply Network") and Game Developer design case study; WitE2 manual ch. 25 (Logistics) and ch. 28 (Production); Supreme Ruler fandom wiki Supply Model + Steam discussions ("The Unit Supply System is Broken"); AGEOD AGEWiki Supply page + forum threads.
key_takeaways: Compute detailed supply lazily: run the full hub/rail-graph flow solver ONLY inside active war theaters (a declared front region), and let the rest of the 4,600-province world run on regional aggregate logistics that piggyback on the existing economic-region simulation. A Cold War game is at peace almost everywhere, almost always — this is the single biggest structural difference from HoI4/WitE2, and it is what makes NSB-depth supply affordable at this map scale.

Make military supply throughput a draw on the SAME regional rail-capacity and oil-balance numbers the economy already uses, not a parallel resource. Mobilizing a theater visibly crowds out civilian freight and drains the oil balance — guns-vs-butter emerges for free, and interdiction bombing/sabotage (espionage pillar!) becomes a supply weapon with no new systems.

Player-designed units must carry exactly two supply-relevant derived stats — fuel draw (from motorization/engine choices) and ammo draw (from firepower) — aggregated per formation. This makes the design space real: US-style mechanized divisions are powerful but tethered to ports and railheads; Chinese-style light infantry accept low firepower for near-immunity to interdiction. Korea's actual asymmetry falls out of the unit designer instead of being scripted.

Ports are the amphibious mechanic. Over-the-beach supply is a small, wasting allowance (days, not months); captured port capacity is the real number. Incheon is then a systems-native masterstroke — you land where a port exists AND where holding it severs the single rail trunk feeding the enemy's southern front — not an event.

Legibility over fidelity: track tonnage internally (WitE2-style flow math is fine), but surface exactly three unit states — Supplied / Strained / Cut — with a UoC-style map overlay showing the path each formation's supply takes and where it would be cut. If a player can't predict the effect of taking one province on the enemy's supply state, the encirclement game doesn't exist.

Zero recurring player micro: no manual convoys (Supreme Ruler), no wagon shuttling (AGEOD), no train-count babysitting (HoI4). Player logistics decisions are infrastructure investments (rail upgrades, hub/port construction, pre-war stockpiles) and one-time route/priority settings; resolution is automatic, once per game-day, not hourly — supply is a daily-integrated quantity even though combat ticks hourly.

systems.domain: Hearts of Iron IV: No Step Back — hub-and-spoke railway supply
systems.how_it_works: Supply originates at the capital and flows outward along a railway graph to supply hubs (fixed map nodes; buildable at ~pre-set locations). Rail segments have levels 1-5 that cap flow; every active hub consumes trains from a national train pool (hubs without nearby divisions pass flow through and cost nothing). Each hub projects supply into surrounding provinces with range/amount falling off with distance and terrain; assigning trucks (motorization level 0-2) extends range and amount at the cost of trucks and fuel. Provinces also have small local supply from population + state infrastructure. Ports act as hubs fed by convoys for overseas theaters. Divisions draw a supply weight (sum of battalion needs); shortfall causes attrition, reduced combat stats, and slowed movement. Hubs can be bombed, captured (flipping their feed direction after a delay), and railways damaged/repaired.
systems.strengths: Made encirclement and deep battle real in a mainstream GSG: cutting one rail trunk behind a front actually starves it. Infrastructure becomes a war-planning layer — players genuinely study the Soviet rail map before Barbarossa. Hub capture with a conversion delay creates operational tempo (you can't instantly use enemy rails — gauge conversion, historically true for Korea too). Train/truck pools tie logistics to industrial output.
systems.weaknesses: Post-launch community verdict (Paradox forums, 'Better Supply' mod with large uptake): tedium without decisions. Hub locations are mostly fixed, so 'play' collapses into clicking motorization-level buttons and building rail to the same choke provinces every run. AI can't handle it — AI armies starve, and player allies become liabilities. Low-infrastructure regions (China, USSR east) became near-unplayable division-cap zones, felt punishing rather than strategic. Numbers are opaque: players couldn't answer 'why is this tile at 40% supply' without YouTube guides. Micromanaging at lowest speed during offensives was a common complaint.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT the topology, fix the two failures. The capital→rail-graph→hub→radius model is the right skeleton for 4,600 provinces because it means supply is computed on a graph of ~dozens of nodes per theater, not per-province. But (1) only instantiate the graph inside active war theaters — peacetime provinces need no supply solve at all; (2) make hub placement/port development a player investment with real siting choices (this IS Cold War statecraft: building the Karakoram highway, rail to Murmansk), not fixed nodes; (3) feed the graph from our existing regional rail-capacity number so military flow competes with economic freight — NSB's train pool gestured at this, we can do it natively. Keep hub capture-and-convert delay: it's the Korea rail-gauge/repair story.

systems.domain: Unity of Command 1 & 2 — supply as THE core gameplay
systems.how_it_works: UoC1: supply is 'thrown' from map-edge sources along rail/road, with range measured in movement points; enemy control of a single rail hex severs everything downstream. Units unsupplied for one turn lose attack capability and take penalties; by turn two-plus they visibly wither ('melt before your infantry' — even elite panzers). UoC2 adds three explicit states (supplied / low supply / isolated), mobile depots and trucks as scarce placeable assets, HQ-based emergency supply drops, and air/naval supply for bridgeheads. The overlay shows the exact supplied network at all times; scenario time limits force you to win via cutting supply rather than frontal attrition.
systems.strengths: The gold standard for making logistics the strategy rather than the bookkeeping. Total legibility: one glance shows what's supplied and what one hex-capture would sever — so players plan encirclements the way real staffs did. The 'strangle, don't smash' incentive structure (time limits + supply-kill being faster than combat-kill) is exactly the limited-war grammar we want: victory by position and severance, not annihilation. Zero recurring micro; the design case study literature repeatedly cites it for capturing operational art 'without drowning the player in detail.'
systems.weaknesses: It's a hand-crafted scenario puzzle game: fixed sources, small maps, turn-based, no economy behind the supply. Doesn't answer how supply is produced, or scale to a persistent 41-year sandbox. Its brutally fast starvation (2-3 turns to combat-uselessness) is tuned for 10-turn scenarios and would feel arbitrary in real-time. Some players found optimal play degenerated into 'chase the rail hex' to the exclusion of combat.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the presentation and incentive layer wholesale. Three supply states, a map overlay that renders each formation's live supply path and highlights cut-points, and starvation that degrades combat power before it kills units (slower than UoC — think 1-2 weeks to combat-ineffective, months to destruction, matching Chosin/Pusan reality). Crucially, UoC proves our escalation-ceiling thesis: when total destruction is off the table (their time limits, our escalation caps), cutting supply becomes the dominant and most interesting win condition. Limited war under a ceiling should be won the UoC way — sever, encircle, force withdrawal — which also keeps casualty counts (escalation pressure) down. This is the model that makes 'total war is the failure state' playable.

systems.domain: Gary Grigsby's War in the East 2 — depot/freight tonnage simulation
systems.how_it_works: Full tonnage-flow model resolved in an automated logistics phase. National supply sources generate freight (2.5M tons per source per supply phase); freight moves along the rail grid with per-hex tonnage caps (30,000 tons/turn dual-track, 12,000 single-track) into a hierarchy of depots (levels 1-4) at towns/cities/ports; railyard capacity gates throughput (a level-2 railyard = 20k capacity, 20x that at a national supply source hex). Units within range of a stocked depot draw generic freight, converted on receipt into supplies/fuel/ammo/replacements; the last miles are covered by unit-organic and army-level truck pools that deplete and must be replaced by production. Rail must be converted/repaired hex-by-hex by rail-repair units. Air resupply and port-to-port sea freight exist under the same tonnage accounting.
systems.strengths: The most faithful model on the market: Barbarossa's culmination, the Stalingrad airlift's inadequacy, and mud-season paralysis all emerge from the numbers rather than scripts. Depot hierarchy + last-mile trucks is the correct real-world decomposition (rail for bulk, trucks for the gap — this is literally the 8th Army's Korea problem). Because the flow solve is automated, a 25,000-hex map with hundreds of units stays computable; the player's levers (depot priorities 0-4, rail repair sequencing) are genuinely strategic.
systems.weaknesses: Legendary opacity — the logistics chapter is ~40 pages of manual, and the community meme is that you need a spreadsheet to know why your spearhead stalled. Depot-priority micromanagement each turn is real tedium for optimizers. Freight-as-universal-currency hides the distinct strategic characters of fuel vs ammo. Audience: thousands of players, not millions. UI shows you everything and explains nothing.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT the math, bury the presentation. Use WitE2's decomposition internally — regional freight generation (from our industry sim), per-rail-segment tonnage caps (our rail-capacity concept, made segment-wise only inside theaters), depot/hub stock levels, organic truck last-mile — because it's proven to produce historical outcomes from first principles. But keep exactly TWO commodities visible in supply flow: fuel (drawn against our regional oil balance — mechanized armies are oil-hungry, and oil embargo/interdiction becomes a war-winning lever, very Cold War) and general supply (everything else, sourced from regional industrial output where coal/steel already gate production upstream, so we don't re-track them in logistics). Never show the player tonnage tables; show fulfillment percentages and the three UoC states. Depot priorities should default to automatic with an optional per-front override, never per-depot clicking.

systems.domain: Supreme Ruler series — per-unit fuel/ammo tracking
systems.how_it_works: Every individual unit (battalion-scale, thousands on map) carries its own fuel and ammunition stores, depleted by movement and combat at rates from the unit's spec sheet. Supply propagates outward from cities/bases through connected road/infrastructure hexes as a decaying field; units in supplied hexes replenish automatically, drawing on national resource stockpiles (the game also runs full market economics for petroleum, ammo as a produced good, etc.). Dedicated supply-truck and transport-aircraft units can be manually shuttled to top up units beyond the field's reach.
systems.weaknesses: The cautionary tale. Community threads are titled 'The Unit Supply System is Broken': armor burns fuel/ammo faster than manual truck shuttles can replenish, deep offensives stall for opaque reasons, and the fix is hand-managing individual supply trucks — pure bookkeeping hell. The supply field is invisible-ish and poorly explained, so failure reads as bugs rather than strategy. At thousands of units, per-unit state tracking gives no strategic texture the field couldn't give: nobody plans encirclements in Supreme Ruler, they just suffer logistics. AI handles none of it.
systems.strengths: Proves per-unit fuel/ammo bookkeeping CAN run at massive scale technically (real-time, whole-world map) — performance is not the blocker. Fuel-as-national-resource linking the war machine to petroleum markets is genuinely ahead of its time and exactly our pillar. Unit spec sheets defining consumption rates is a natural fit for design-your-own-units.
systems.lesson_for_1950: AVOID the architecture, salvage two ideas. Do not track fuel/ammo per unit-entity and never create player-driven resupply units. Salvage: (1) consumption rates as first-class outputs of the unit designer — every design choice (engine, gun caliber, armor weight) rolls up to fuel-draw/day and ammo-draw-in-combat numbers shown on the design sheet, so logistics burden is a visible design tradeoff, not a surprise; (2) fuel drawn from the national/regional oil balance we already simulate, so a mechanized doctrine is a standing claim on the oil economy even in peacetime (training, readiness) — which is historically why oil was THE Cold War resource. Aggregate consumption at the formation level (corps/army), resolved daily.

systems.domain: AGEOD engine — supply wagons and two-pass push distribution
systems.how_it_works: Turn-based (WEGO) engine. Supply is produced in cities/depots and 'pushed' outward each turn through the region graph in an automated multi-pass algorithm, decaying with distance and blocked by enemy zones of control; armies in supply range (roughly 3-5 regions from a depot or level-3+ city) stay topped up. Each force also has organic supply-wagon elements holding several days of supply and ammo as a buffer for operating beyond the net; depots can be built by player action to extend the net. Attrition from being out of supply is the dominant killer in these games, dwarfing battle losses (historically correct for the 19th century settings).
systems.strengths: The push-with-decay model is cheap, fully automatic, and produces correct strategic behavior: armies tethered to depots, raids on the enemy's rear that actually matter, campaigns that culminate. The wagon-buffer concept — a formation carries N days of operating reserve, letting it lunge beyond the net before withering — is a clean, legible mechanic that creates exactly the 'operational clock' feeling (you have X days to take the objective before you must pause or wither). Attrition-dominance rewards maneuver over battle-seeking.
systems.weaknesses: The push algorithm is opaque (supply sometimes 'goes the wrong way'; forum threads are full of confusion), and in edge cases (sieges) players resorted to manually shuttling wagon units — micro the design explicitly tried to avoid. Distance-decay without hard throughput caps means no real chokepoints: you can't model 'this single rail line can only feed 12 divisions,' which is the heart of Korea-scale logistics. No meaningful interaction with an economy.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the wagon-buffer as our formation-level mechanic: every formation (with capacity set in the unit/formation designer — organic truck battalions cost industry and oil) carries N days of supply. Inside the hub network it stays full; beyond it, the buffer drains, giving amphibious landings and armored thrusts an explicit, UI-visible countdown ('supplies for 9 more days'). This is Incheon's X-Corps and Chromite's tension in one number, and it's also the natural knob for doctrine asymmetry (Chinese formations: low draw, small buffer, short violent offensives — their historical one-week 'phase offensives' emerge from the math). REJECT pure distance-decay as the network model — we need hard per-segment throughput caps (WitE2/our rail capacity) so cutting a line or bombing a bridge has calculable, dramatic effect.

systems.domain: Amphibious and port supply — the Incheon requirement (HoI4 naval supply, UoC2 naval/air supply, WitE2 ports)
systems.how_it_works: HoI4: overseas theaters are fed through ports acting as supply hubs, throughput scaled by port level (1-10) and convoy availability; convoys are interdictable by subs/air; naval invasions initially supplied at a trickle over the beach until a port is captured (later DLC added buildable floating harbors). UoC2: beachhead units draw limited naval/air supply — enough to survive briefly, not to operate. WitE2: sea freight moves port-to-port under the same tonnage accounting, gated by port capacity and shipping; amphibious ops carry limited organic supply and must link to a functioning port quickly.
systems.strengths: All three converge on the same correct structure: beach supply = small wasting allowance, port capacity = the real constraint, sea line = interdictable. This makes amphibious operations self-limiting without any special rules — you cannot Sealion because you cannot feed it, but you CAN Incheon because Incheon has a port and the defender's rear rail net passes nearby. Convoy interdiction gives navies and submarines a supply-war role (our espionage/limited-war space: 'accidental' sinkings, mining — escalation-ceiling content).
systems.weaknesses: HoI4's version was long derided because pre-NSB naval invasions were nearly supply-free (Sealion meme), and post-NSB the AI can't manage overseas supply at all. Floating harbors made port capture optional, deflating the mechanic. If beach supply is too generous, amphibious ops become teleporting doom-stacks; too stingy, and the mechanic is decorative because no player ever lands.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT with hard numbers: formations land with their AGEOD-style organic buffer (N days) plus a per-beachhead trickle from naval transport capacity; capturing a port converts the beachhead to a real hub whose throughput = port level minus damage (defenders demolish ports — Wonsan, Hungnam). Sea lines are graph edges like rail, capped by sealift pools and interdictable. Tie the vertical slice's victory condition to this: Incheon succeeds in our sim iff (a) port captured near-intact within the buffer window, and (b) holding Seoul severs the single rail trunk to the Pusan perimeter — both statements our supply graph can natively evaluate. No floating harbors in 1950; port seizure must stay mandatory, because that constraint is what makes WHERE to land a strategic decision.

reports.games: Rule the Waves 2/3 (Matrix/NWS), Hearts of Iron IV + No Step Back tank designer / By Blood Alone plane designer (Paradox), Supreme Ruler Ultimate / 2020 (BattleGoat), Shadow Empire (VR Designs/Matrix), War in the Pacific: Admiral's Edition and War in the East 2 (Matrix/2by3), Victoria 2/3 (Paradox), Aurora 4X (reference point for over-deep equipment design). Sources consulted: RTW3 manual + Naval Gazing review + Matrix dev diary #3 (ship design), HoI4 wiki/EIP/PCGamesN meta guides and Steam meta guide threads, Supreme Ruler Fandom wiki (Unit Fabrication, Research, Designs), Shadow Empire Steam/Matrix forum threads on model design and OOB rigidity, WitP:AE Matrix forum threads on TRACOM/pilot pools, Victoria 3 army composition guides and Steam discussions.
key_takeaways: Adopt a two-layer architecture with asymmetric depth: EQUIPMENT design is the deep, player-authored layer (design the tank/interceptor/SSBN generation, ~1-2 big decisions per domain per decade, RTW-style budget tradeoffs against steel/oil/military_stock); the FORMATION layer is template-LITE — a curated set of doctrine-era archetypes (Pentomic, ROAD, Motor-Rifle, airborne, etc.) whose equipment slots and manpower-quality mix the player tunes, not a free-form HoI4 width puzzle. This matches theater-level command: theaters consume formations, formations consume designs, designs consume the economy you already built.

Retooling friction is the single most important anti-degeneracy lever: HoI4 proves that per-line efficiency (10%→50% cap, ~90% retained on variant, as low as 10% on full switch) is what makes design decisions COMMITMENTS instead of spreadsheet churn. Your planned production-efficiency/retooling system should be the spine that equipment design plugs into — a new tank generation is a factory-retooling event with a multi-year efficiency valley, which naturally produces the real Cold War rhythm of equipment generations and mixed-vintage armies.

Design stats must stay few, soft, and uncertain: RTW succeeds because designs are conceptual (speed/armor/guns/range against a tonnage+budget cap) and their true combat value is revealed in battle; HoI4's 9-module designer degenerated into solved armor-stacking/cheap-hull metas within weeks. Give designs ~5-6 opposed axes (firepower, protection, mobility, cost, reliability, logistics footprint), let doctrine and crew quality modify them, and accept espionage-driven uncertainty about enemy designs — that IS the Cold War intelligence game.

Manpower quality is a second capital stock, not a slider: model conscript intake from your demographic cohorts (rural/urban/educated feeding different arms), a decaying trained-reserve pool of discharged conscripts (Soviet Category A/B/C mobilization tiers are a ready-made design), and an officer/NCO corps that grows slowly from the educated cohort and is destroyed quickly (purges, attrition). WitP:AE shows pool-quality systems create real strategic decisions; it also shows they must be policy-level (set training throughput and reserve categories), never individual-level management.

Never require re-design or re-research to do logistically trivial things: Shadow Empire's most-cited failure is needing a new researched model to issue existing body armor to existing infantry, and Supreme Ruler's is an auto-build minister mass-producing bridging units. Upgrading formations to a new equipment mark should be an automatic, rate-limited flow (old mark cascades to reserves/exports/clients), and any AI assistance must be transparent and overridable.

Exploit the Cold-War-specific payoffs no WW2 game has: designed equipment is also an INFLUENCE and ESPIONAGE object — export marks for client states (monomarks like the MiG-21/T-55 as arms-diplomacy currency), captured/defected equipment revealing design stats (MiG-15 in Korea, Ivy League intel coups), dual-capable systems interacting with escalation ceilings, and mothball/readiness states (RTW's 20% mothball cost, working-up crew quality) driving the mobilization-signaling game that brinkmanship needs.

systems.domain: Rule the Waves 2/3 — budget-constrained equipment design over decades
systems.how_it_works: Player is a navy department, not a country: a monthly budget (moved by prestige, tensions, government) must cover construction, active-fleet maintenance, R&D (capped ~12% of budget, max efficiency at ~10%), and readiness states — mothballed ships cost 20% of active maintenance but have poorly trained crews and need long work-up; ships under repair cost ~2x. Ship design is conceptual, not modular: tonnage, speed, range, armor scheme, gun layout, freeboard/accommodation traded inside a displacement and budget cap, with tech (and espionage) gating what's designable. Designs live 20-30 years, get one or two refits, and fight in auto-resolved-or-tactical battles where their soft stats actually matter. Smaller/cheaper designs buy quantity; over-ambitious ones eat the whole budget.
systems.strengths: The gold standard for 'design connects to economy': every design decision is a budget decision, and the long service life makes design a strategic identity choice (you LIVE with your 1910 battlecruisers in 1925). Low decision frequency + high stakes = no tedium. Uncertainty about rival designs (revealed by intel or combat) keeps the meta unsolvable. Readiness tiers (active/reserve/mothball) create a genuine peacetime-posture game.
systems.weaknesses: The economy behind the budget is a black box — no industry, resources, or demographics, so it can't teach us the integration layer, only the design layer. UI-heavy and opaque for new players (Steam threads: 'intimidating'). Auto-generated rival designs occasionally produce nonsense. No land component at all.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the design philosophy wholesale for the equipment layer: few, soft, opposed stats under a hard cost cap; multi-decade service lives; refit/modernization passes instead of constant redesign; espionage-gated knowledge of enemy designs. ADOPT readiness states (active/category-B/mothball with crew-quality consequences) — they plug directly into your brinkmanship pillar as visible mobilization signals. Replace RTW's abstract budget with your real one: a design's cost should decompose into steel/oil/military_stock draw and factory-line time, so 'can I afford the M60 program' is answered by the economy sim you already have.

systems.domain: HoI4 production lines — efficiency, retooling, and the economy hookup
systems.how_it_works: Civilian/military factory split; each military production line produces one equipment design and has its own efficiency that starts at 10% and grows toward a 50% cap (both modifiable by tech/doctrine), taking up to ~500 days uncapped. Switching a line to a variant of the same chassis retains up to ~90% of accrued efficiency; switching to a different equipment family drops it as low as 10%. Resources (steel, tungsten, oil...) are per-line inputs; shortages cut output. Output accumulates in national equipment stockpiles that divisions draw from and lend-lease/exports drain.
systems.strengths: This is the best-in-class model of exactly what you've already planned (equipment production efficiency + retooling friction): it makes design churn expensive, makes early standardization vs. late superiority a real strategic tradeoff, and makes industrial planning FEEL like WW2/Cold War procurement. The stockpile-buffer pattern (lines fill a national pool, formations draw from it) decouples design cadence from front-line micromanagement — ideal for theater-level command.
systems.weaknesses: Line micromanagement scales badly for majors (dozens of lines to babysit); players learn to game efficiency with 'variant laundering'; resources are static map dots rather than a live economy; and because divisions only care about equipment COUNTS, the stockpile hides quality (a pool of 1936 and 1943 guns is one number until upgrade priority menus get involved — a chronic UI pain point).
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the line/stockpile/retooling triad as the spine — your military_stock accumulation is already this. ADAPT: (1) make stockpiles per-equipment-generation, not fungible, so mixed-vintage forces exist and old marks cascade downward to reserves and arms exports (a Cold War influence mechanic HoI4 lacks); (2) tie line inputs to your real steel/oil balances and regional power grids so a bombed grid or oil embargo actually starves specific programs; (3) cap the number of concurrent programs by nation size/era so the player runs ~5-15 lines, never 60 — procurement should read like a defense budget, not a spreadsheet farm.

systems.domain: HoI4 templates + tank/plane designer — the BOTH-layered endgame and its degenerate metas
systems.how_it_works: Layer 1 (since launch): the division designer — free-form templates from battalions/support companies with combat width, org, soft/hard attack; the whole army instantiates templates and auto-follows edits. Layer 2 (No Step Back 2021 / By Blood Alone 2022): equipment designers — a tank is up to 9 modules (gun, turret, armor, engine, special) on a chassis, producing the stats the template's battalions inherit. So the endgame HoI4 stack is: module → equipment design → production line → stockpile → template → division → army.
systems.strengths: Template-instancing is a superb altitude mechanic: design once, army follows, one edit upgrades everything — exactly right for a player who commands at theater level. The two layers give distinct fantasies (engineer vs. force-planner). Community engagement with design meta is enormous — it demonstrably sells and retains.
systems.weaknesses: Both layers went degenerate. Templates: years of solved 7/2 and 40-width metas (patched into a width-per-terrain table players just look up — 15w defense, 25/30/35/40 by terrain), 'space marines' exploits, and Steam threads titled 'templates driving me insane' — free-form composition + hard combat-width math = a solvable puzzle with one right answer. Equipment designer: armor/piercing threshold stacking and cheap-chassis spam were solved within weeks (EIP/meta guides converge on 2-3 builds); module count (9 slots x many parts) creates option noise, not decisions. The two layers also DOUBLE the churn: every new module tempts a redesign of both tank and template.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT, don't adopt: keep BOTH layers but invert the depth. Equipment layer deep (RTW-style soft stats, few axes), formation layer SHALLOW — a curated menu of historical doctrine archetypes per era (US: triangular → Pentomic '57 → ROAD '63; Soviet: rifle → motor-rifle; plus airborne/marine/security types) where the player chooses the archetype, fills its equipment slots with their designs, and sets manpower-quality policy — no free-form width math to solve. AVOID hard thresholds (armor>piercing binaries) that create stacking metas; use graded lanchester-ish modifiers. Keep HoI4's one killer feature verbatim: edit the formation type once, the whole force upgrades on a rate-limited schedule.

systems.domain: Supreme Ruler — procurement of designs, fabrication, and minister automation (cautionary tale)
systems.how_it_works: Unit designs are researched capabilities (also stealable via espionage, buyable, tradeable) gated by underlying techs. Units are built at constructed fabrication facilities ('fabs' — land/air/naval), consuming money and industrial goods from a commodity economy; more research centers = more parallel projects but enormous cost. A Defense Minister AI can auto-build and auto-manage to fight the scale (thousands of individual battalions on a 1:1-ish map).
systems.strengths: Design-as-tradeable-object is genuinely great for a Cold War game: buying, selling, and stealing designs models the real arms-transfer and espionage economy (licensed MiGs, Toms-to-Iran). Fabs as physical, bombable, province-located industry ties production to geography — which your province/power-grid sim can do even better.
systems.weaknesses: The canonical over-scale failure: no template layer at all, so equipment designs are commanded as thousands of individual units — unplayable without minister AI, and the minister is infamous for pathologies (wiki-documented: mass-producing bridging units because a bridging unit had the highest tech level in the supply class). Design itself is shallow — you research a stat block, you don't author it. Reviews consistently cite tedium and opacity.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT exactly two ideas: (1) designs as first-class diplomatic/espionage objects — exportable under license, stealable by spies, embargo-able — feeding your influence-warfare pillar; (2) physically located production (your provinces/grids already support this — a specific tank plant in Kharkov, a specific shipyard in Groton, targetable in war and legible in peace). AVOID everything else: never let the unit count outrun the player's command altitude, and never paper over a scale problem with an opaque minister AI — if you offer automation, it must execute the player's stated doctrine, visibly.

systems.domain: Shadow Empire — model design fed by a real economy, and the rigidity failure modes
systems.how_it_works: Player designs 'models' (tank, walker, gun...) by allocating tech + design points; a semi-random roll determines final stats (rerolls cost Budget Points; non-structural stats never regress below the current design). Models are then produced from the resource economy (metal, machines, energy, manpower from population) and slotted into OOB formation types (battalion/brigade compositions) that must themselves be unlocked. Replacement flows push new equipment to the front.
systems.strengths: The rare game where unit design sits on top of a REAL simulated economy (resources, logistics points, population) — proof the integration you're planning works and creates drama (a fuel crisis kills your armor doctrine). Randomized design outcomes (Soviet-style 'the prototype disappointed') defeat solved metas and generate stories. Formation-type OOBs keep command at the right altitude.
systems.weaknesses: Two loudly-criticized rigidities: (1) issuing existing equipment to a different troop type requires researching a whole NEW model (the 'kevlar vest' complaint — pure busywork); (2) rigid OOB types mean new capability requires fielding entire fresh green formations instead of re-equipping veterans (the 'RPG infantry' complaint — Matrix forum thread 'I dislike the OOBs'). Managing many model versions is acknowledged tedium; UI is brutal.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT the economy hookup pattern and consider a mild form of design-outcome uncertainty (a new tank program can come in over budget, late, or with a reliability defect discovered in service — very Cold War: M60A2, MBT-70, early Polaris). AVOID both rigidity traps explicitly: equipment must be re-issuable across formation types without re-research, and existing formations must convert to new archetypes/equipment in place, retaining their cadre experience at some readiness cost — that conversion-time-vs-quality tradeoff is itself good gameplay (a motor-rifle division re-equipping is combat-ineffective for months: a real escalation-window consideration).

systems.domain: Manpower quality — WitP:AE pilot pools, WitE2 replacement pools, Victoria 2 officers (trained reserves and officer corps)
systems.how_it_works: WitP:AE: pilots carry ~a dozen skill ratings; a multi-pool system (training classes → replacement pool → group reserves → TRACOM) where 12 monthly classes graduate in sequence, and sending 80+ exp veterans to TRACOM speeds graduation of quality replacements; combat experience only accrues from real missions. WitE2: manpower and armament pools by type, with trained-replacement throughput and experience/morale as the real combat currency. Victoria 2: officers are a POP type grown from educated population via national stockpile spending; mobilization converts civilian POPs to low-quality reserve divisions, gutting the economy while mobilized.
systems.strengths: These systems make QUALITY a slow capital stock you invest in during peace — precisely the Cold War competition (Soviet 2-year conscript churn + huge Category-B/C reserve vs. NATO's long-service professionals). Veterans-as-trainers (TRACOM) is an elegant compounding loop. Victoria's educated-POP→officer pipeline maps 1:1 onto your demographic cohorts. Mobilization-wrecks-the-economy is a built-in escalation cost.
systems.weaknesses: WitP:AE's per-pilot management is legendary tedium (hours per turn for optimizers; forum threads are 90% confusion about which pool does what) — quality systems die when managed at individual granularity. Victoria 2's mobilization was a one-button doomstack with no readiness gradient. All of these under-model reserve DECAY (skills rot; WitP barely, Victoria not at all).
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADOPT at policy granularity only: per-nation (or per-service) sliders/policies for conscript term length, training intensity, and reserve category structure — outputs are pool numbers and quality indices, never individuals. Concretely: rural/urban/educated cohorts feed intake with different aptitude weights (educated → officers/technical branches, competing with your civilian economy's need for the same cohort — a real guns-vs-growth tension); discharged conscripts enter a trained-reserve pool that decays (e.g., full value ~5 years, residual to ~15) and is tapped by mobilization tiers with distinct readiness times and political/escalation visibility; officer corps is a slow stock buildable only from the educated cohort and destructible fast (purge events for authoritarian players — a genuine internal-politics lever). This is the layer that differentiates the superpowers WITHOUT any new unit-design UI.

systems.domain: Victoria 3 / theater-command altitude — what the formation layer must look like when the player doesn't micro
systems.how_it_works: Victoria 3: armies are formations assigned to fronts under generals; player sets composition by unit type and toggles mobilization options (supply/ammo/logistics add-ons that boost performance at economic cost); combat auto-resolves along fronts; unit quality derives from economy (weapons produced by industry, sold to the military as goods).
systems.strengths: Proof that formation-level abstraction + front assignment works for a player operating at grand-strategy altitude, and its 'military consumes goods from the real economy' loop is the same shape as your military_stock design. Mobilization options are a lightweight template system — composition choices without a width puzzle.
systems.weaknesses: Widely criticized as TOO hands-off and opaque: players can't tell what drives offense/defense values (tooltips: 'this is the army's ability on the offense'), can't express operational intent, and mobilization is slow/buggy-feeling; there is no unit design at all, so military investment feels like feeding a black box. This is the failure mode your director's hard requirement exists to prevent.
systems.lesson_for_1950: ADAPT as the floor, not the model: theater-level command (fronts/objectives/postures, Korea-style limited-war ceilings) is right, but the player's authored fingerprint must be visible IN the theater — the theater screen should show 'your' divisions by name/archetype with 'your' equipment marks and quality ratings, and after-action reports should attribute outcomes to design choices ('T-54 frontal armor defeated 90mm at range; US requests 105mm program' — RTW-style feedback). The chain player must always be able to trace: my steel → my line → my tank → my division archetype → this theater's combat power. Legibility of that chain, more than any single mechanic, is what makes 'design your own units' satisfying at theater altitude.
